title: The Best of IFA 2026: AI Dishwashers and Earbuds and Toothbrushes, Oh My!
snippet: Before the IFA 2026 tech event is scheduled to start, we got a sneak peek at all the futuristic devices at the expo.
fullText:
CNET staffers have touched down in Berlin and are on the floor at IFA 2026, one of the world’s largest tech events where the future is on full display. From a camera-equipped dishwasher and Dyson’s largest air purifier yet to a repairable laptop and a speaker designed to soothe you to sleep, we’ve laid eyes on devices that could change how we live, breathe, clean, work and play. 

If you, too, would like to peer into the future and see what’s ahead, this is the best tech we’ve spotted at IFA 2026.

An all-seeing dishwasher

Miele’s Diamond G8 isn’t your average dishwasher.David Watsky/CNET

Miele’s new Diamond G8 dishwasher has an AI-powered internal camera that scans your dishes and decides how to wash them so it doesn’t miss a single spot. Though Home and Kitchen Managing Editor David Watsky, who saw the dishwasher in person, was skeptical about this feature, he was left impressed. 

But the Diamond G8’s scrubbing smarts don’t stop there. If you want the Diamond G8 to run only when electricity is most affordable, it can do that too, waiting for the hours when power costs less. 

Note-taking earbuds

Plaud One: your AI note-taking assistant earbuds. Plaud/CNET

Going beyond its AI note-taking wearable pin and credit card-like device that you can attach to your phone, Plaud launched the Plaud One earbuds to capture and transcribe your conversations and calls. You can even talk to Plaud’s AI by saying, “Hey Plaud,” and then ask it your questions or give it directives. 

“We’d always recommend informing people that you’re using a recording device, and it’s important to note that recording phone calls without permission from all participants can be illegal in some states,” principal writer Katie Collins wrote when covering the Plaud One announcement. 

A robot vacuum that seals itself to carpet

The Roomba Max 875 Combo is all about clean carpet.iRobot

While robot vacuums are great for taking the effort out of keeping your floors clean, CNET’s testing has found that they don’t offer the same suction power as traditional vacuums. iRobot aims to improve on that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which uses SealForce technology to seal itself to carpet and better suction up spots that need extra cleaning. 

In a video call with Home and Robotics Editor Ajay Kumar prior to IFA 2026, Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said SealForce is like pressing harder with a traditional vacuum to thoroughly clean a specific patch of carpet, but in a robot vacuum format. 

A smart ring puts contactless payments at your fingertips

Imagine how cool it will feel to use your ring for contactless payments.Circular

In addition to having the health-tracking capabilities we expect of smart rings, Circular has added contactless payments, a feature typically found on smartwatches and smartphones, to its new subscription-free Ring 3 Pro and Ring 3 Slim. When covering the launch, principal writer Vanessa Hand Orellana wrote that the company also gave both rings haptic vibration alerts, a feature previously available on its first Circular Ring, along with advanced sleep metrics, glucose trend estimates and access to its AI health coach.

A laptop built to be repaired

The Vero 16 comes with its own repair guide.Acer/CNET

With its new fourth-generation Vero 16, Acer brings the “right to repair” conversation into focus, as CNET writer Tyler Graham explained that the modular laptop is designed to let users easily upgrade its components themselves. There’s even a repair guide engraved on it to help with these swaps.

The Vero 16 didn’t come alone, as it was announced alongside Acer’s compact 14-inch Swift Blade 14 and sleek 16-inch Swift Air 16. 

A speaker that lulls you to sleep

Sleep has never sounded so sweet.Katie Collins/CNET

Alongside its Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro with a touchscreen case, Anker introduced the SleepLab Pro speaker, which uses radar to track your sleep, breathing and heart rate, then customizes its audio to help you drift off to dreamland and stay there. “It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table,” Collins wrote when describing the device. It also triples as a sunrise alarm clock and a nightlight that glows in a range of shades. 

A non-Pro SleepLab has the same features, minus radar sleep tracking.  

Dyson’s largest air purifier

Air purifier or Dune sandworm? You decide.Dyson

The new Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde (try to say that five times fast) was designed to purify multiple rooms using the company’s most powerful processor. As Kumar put it, it looks like a Dune sandworm with its nozzle head that can be rotated and tilted. While operating quietly, the purifier can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns for a breath of fresh air.

Lenovo’s first rollable work laptop

Lenovo is on a roll. Josh Goldman/CNET

Lenovo’s Project Swan concept is a laptop that expands horizontally at the touch of a button, transforming its display from 14 to 17 inches. But unlike the Legion Pro Rollable Graham spotted at CES 2026, this isn’t a gaming laptop – it’s for work. Perfect for work trips when you want a more compact 14-inch display for travel, but a 17-inch for getting the job done (or watching movies during your downtime). 

Dyson’s first toothbrush

Plaque begone!Tara Brown/CNET

title: FBI investigates as hackers sell digital scans of 153M drivers licenses
snippet: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more. The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … more…
fullText:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more.

The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … 

Krebs on Security was able to confirm the authenticity of the claim made by the cybercriminals as they were able to provide a scan of his own driving license, with other victims likewise confirming their scans were correct.

A new identity theft service [dubbed Nexus] launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada […] The people behind Nexus claim the license images are coming from an active breach at “a major identity verification company” whose customers include multiple Fortune 500 companies.

KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

The report says that the ID verification company appears to be one based in Louisiana. The criminals claim that they still have access to the source of these scans, a claim supported by their adding almost 400,000 new ones within the past 24 hours.

There are indications suggesting that at least some of the data was stolen from a verification service used by rental car company Hertz. The report points to a New Orleans-based company as a potential source, and that company’s client list includes Hertz, Target, Fedex, Motorola Solutions, Jack Henry, and Caesars Entertainment. There are many more details in the full report.

9to5Mac’s Take

The irony of criminals being able to hack an identity verification service in order to provide documents that can be used for identity theft would be amusing if it weren’t so serious. This type of breach is depressingly common.

It was recently estimated that online scams cost Americans almost $150 billion last year as the number of cyber scams continue to increase dramatically.

title: Unusual timing of Mac mini and Mac Studio updates all about AI, claims report
snippet: Apple surprised many when it quietly announced updated Mac mini and Mac Studio models shortly before its September event. We would normally have expected these announcements to be part of that event. One strong theory is that the company may be making a lot of big announcements in its ‘Surprise and shine‘ keynote, and therefore wanted to get these updates out of the way beforehand. But a new report presents another theory … more…
fullText:
Apple surprised many when it quietly announced updated Mac mini and Mac Studio models shortly before its September event. We would normally have expected these announcements to be part of that event.

One strong theory is that the company may be making a lot of big announcements in its ‘Surprise and shine‘ keynote, and therefore wanted to get these updates out of the way beforehand. But a new report presents another theory … 

Announcing the new Mac mini and Mac Studio models just a fortnight ahead of the September 9th event seemed surprising. Why not wait the extra couple of weeks and do it properly, rather than just via press releases?

The Information says that the decision was made because the company was taken by surprise by the level of demand for the models for AI applications, and with some configurations unavailable for months, Apple brought the announcements forward for this reason.

9to5Mac’s Take

There’s certainly no doubt that the power of Apple Silicon has made both the Mac mini and Mac Studio popular options for those wanting to run AI models locally. For example, we’ve seen researchers use Thunderbolt 5 to turn four Mac Studios into an extremely powerful AI cluster.

I can also believe that Apple did not initially predict the scale of demand this was going to generate.

What seems less likely, however, is the idea that two weeks makes any worthwhile difference to the situation. To me, it’s just too small a gap for this to be a credible explanation. Personally, I think the existing theory we outlined is the more likely one.

Apple will want to make a very big fuss about the launch of its first foldable iPhone and also ensure that the iPhone 18 Pro isn’t seen as an also-ran. If Apple does indeed unveil the HomePad smart home hub as we expect, that too will be a major announcement.

We then need to add in a new Apple TV and HomePod mini 2 – both with Siri AI capabilities – two new Apple Watch models, and potentially new AirPods too. That’s a lot of announcements for a single keynote, so I could absolutely understand wanting to launch the new Mac desktops beforehand.

title: Qualcomm’s upcoming premium chip has Adreno ‘Neural Fusion’ GPU
snippet: Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. more…
fullText:
Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU.

Qualcomm’s next SoC will be the first chipset to feature dedicated AI GPU cores in the graphics pipeline. These so-called “Matrix Cores” sit snugly in each of the three 1.45GHz GPU slices on the new Adreno GPU. Qualcomm says they act as dedicated local hardware to “run advanced AI models directly inside the graphics pipeline.”

The Snapdragon chip’s Adreno GPU will also feature a dedicated 18MB HPM (High Performance Memory) cache. That capacity sounds humble, but Qualcomm says its HPM “provides large, low-latency memory directly to the GPU, allowing tile-based rendering,

frame buffers, and compute workloads to remain local to the graphics subsystem.”

Both components in the new core architecture help make up the entirety of the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. For the end user, it means a 40% power improvement with the technology enabled. The company detailed in its press release how developing an SoC with AI processing done in closer proximity to the GPU means less latency and better efficiency.

	

The trick is keeping the work close to the silicon. Adreno Matrix Cores handle AI models right where the graphics happen, and the 18MB of Adreno High Performance Memory holds the heavy data—tiles, frame buffers, compute—on-chip so it isn’t constantly shuffling back and forth to system memory. Less movement means lower latency and better efficiency, which translates into gaming sessions that last longer.

For the time being, Unity and Unreal Engine have already integrated Qualcomm’s Neural Fusion stack.

The end result should be improved graphics quality with “upscaled images, stable frame rates, and improved efficiency through AI-enhanced rendering built directly into the Snapdragon

graphics pipeline,” as Qualcomm puts it.

Snapdragon Summit is scheduled for September 22-24, and more is set to be announced regarding the new chip’s NPU.

title: John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO: Here’s the latest
snippet: Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make. more…
fullText:
Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make.

Luca Maestri

Bloomberg reports that Luca Maestri is stepping down as Apple’s “Corporate Services” leader. Maestri served as Apple CFO until January 2025, when he stepped down to take on a smaller role. As head of Corporate Services, Maestri oversaw information systems and technology, information security, and real estate and development.

According to today’s report, Maestri left that job “in recent weeks.” He is, however, still on Apple’s payroll. His only remaining responsibility is “hosting a popular class at Apple University, an in-house program for teaching Apple’s ways to rising executives and employees.”

Bloomberg says that Maestri’s Corporate Services tasks have been shifted to CFO Kevan Parekh.

Adrian Perica

Mark Gurman points out that Apple’s new Leadership page excludes Adrian Perica, its head of mergers and acquisitions.

Apple’s new leadership page also excludes Adrian Perica, the company’s head of mergers and acquisitions. It remains unclear where he will shift within Apple. Bloomberg reported on Sunday that he would likely be dropped by Ternus as a direct report and could split his responsibilities across Apple’s services and finance teams.

It’s possible this signals a change to Apple’s strategy for mergers and acquisitions. Some analysts expect Ternus to be more aggressive in making bigger acquisitions.

A change to how Apple manages outgoing executives

Gurman also says that “people in and around Apple” expect Ternus to change how the company handles outgoing executives. While Cook made a habit of retaining executives in smaller roles, like Maestri, Gurman says “Ternus may be less likely to continue using this approach.”

More tidbits

Ternus officially joined X today, and his first tweet was an all-lowercase “hello” with no punctuation. The post was quoted by marketing exec Greg Joswiak, who wrote: “Hello, indeed. More to say September 9.”

Gurman says Apple is hosting an event at Apple Park today “to introduce John Ternus as its new CEO to employees and to again celebrate Tim Cook’s tenure.”

Laura Legros, a former Apple VP who Ternus recruited out of retirement last month, will reportedly serve in a “Chief of Staff” style role. Cook did not have a person like this around him, according to Gurman.

snippet: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API. more…
fullText:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour. 

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

title: YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required
snippet: Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube. more…
fullText:
Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube.

As described in an announcement post on the YouTube support forums, Google is rolling out some big changes to how YouTube on your smartphone interacts with your television. The company is describing your device as a “companion” now, even ditching the classic Cast icon for something a little more generic. It’s a change that, based on Reddit threads, seemingly entered testing earlier in 2026, and is now ready for a full rollout. 

It’s not just a new way to describe pairing your devices, though. With this refresh, casting videos from your phone to a television now sounds like it has a whole lot less friction, thanks in part to a shift on completely relying on account-based management. These changes include:

No longer requiring both devices to be on a shared Wi-Fi network to cast. Instead, users will need to be signed in on the same account on both devices.

The ability to like videos, leave comments, and subscribe to channels while the video plays in the background.

The option to consume YouTube Shorts content on your phone while a different, full-length video plays on your television.

A built-in “Play on different device” option found within the menu button on every video listed in your homepage feed.

There are, of course, some caveats to these upgrades, and it primarily revolves around the shift to forcing account-based pairing between devices. While this should work wonders for private viewing sessions — i.e., casting a video from your own phone to your own television to watch either independently or with someone else in the room — it’s unclear if this completely removes the ability to cast over Wi-Fi, something that’s genuinely useful in larger gatherings with multiple participants. That’s a pretty common use case for watching YouTube on a television, so I’m hoping generic Cast support continues to exist in this format. Otherwise, this feels like a particularly anti-social change from Google.

	

Generally, though, these are all steps in the right direction, taking a lot of the existing Cast elements and simply streamlining them for a more modern second-screen experience. That “Play on different device” option, for example, appears to be pretty similar to the current casting menu, but won’t require you to begin playing a video on your phone prior to beaming it to your TV. Personally, browsing Shorts while watching a full-length video on your television sounds pretty overwhelming to me, but it’s certainly Google meeting modern viewers where they’re already at.

Today’s announcement did not include a specific rollout window, but it does sound like it’ll be coming to a mobile device near you very, very soon.

fullText:
In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade.

Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 arrive today

In Anthropic’s world, Fable is Claude’s most capable model. Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus are the small, medium, and large models below Fable. 

“Claude Fable 5.1 sets a new standard on coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks,” Anthropic says. The company says the new model has a higher level of performance compared to Fable 5.

Anthropic also says Fable 5.1 “achieves similar or better results than Fable 5 at a much lower cost” when set to low or medium effort.

More from Anthropic below:

Fable 5.1 avoids shortcuts that result in poorer-quality work, and it’s smart enough to fix the root causes of software issues. For example, in testing by the investment firm Millennium, Fable 5.1 found the cause of a rare crash on their internal systems that none of their engineers (or any other model) had been able to explain after several years of trying.

In addition to Fable 5.1, Anthropic is also releasing Mythos 5.1 for users with Mythos access.

“Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but with different levels of safeguards,” Anthropic explains. “Fable 5.1 is generally available, while Mythos 5.1 is available only through our trusted access programs; its safeguards are specifically designed to support work in cybersecurity and the life sciences.”

Here’s pricing data for Fable 5.1:

Fable 5.1 will cost an estimated 25% less than Fable 5 for typical workloads, wherever usage is billed by token. This is because we’re reducing our pricing on cache reads (where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored). For highly agentic work, the savings will often be much larger—up to approximately 45%.

In terms of pricing, Anthropic says it has “reduced the price of Fable 5.1’s cache reads (where the model reuses context it has already processed) wherever usage is billed by token, such as on our API.” The company says this “leads to a substantial reduction in the overall cost of running the model.” Pricing is otherwise unchanged from Fable 5.

You can learn much more in the announcement post here.

title: Qualcomm backs Ultrahuman in $70M round on bet to turn smart rings into computers
snippet: Ultrahuman is targeting a $200 million annual revenue run rate by January 2027 as it builds a new Qualcomm-powered smart ring.
fullText:
Ultrahuman, an Indian startup best known for making smart rings, has raised $70 million in a new funding round that includes backing from Qualcomm’s venture arm, as it looks beyond sleep and health tracking to build a ring that can run software on the device and eventually power everything from AI interactions to games.

The round values Bengaluru-based Ultrahuman at $365 million, about 3x its $120 million valuation in 2023, a person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch.

Qualcomm Ventures participated in the financing alongside U.S. diagnostics giant Labcorp, Alpha Wave, Blume Ventures, Nexus Venture Partners, and Alteria Capital. The round includes $65 million in primary equity and $5 million in debt, Ultrahuman founder and CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview.

Ultrahuman is also working with Qualcomm on a new ring that will use the U.S. chipmaker’s silicon, Kumar told TechCrunch. The startup currently uses chips from Nordic Semiconductor in its rings and plans to continue using them alongside Qualcomm’s technology. The added computing power will allow more software and algorithms to run directly on the ring, reducing its reliance on a phone or the cloud, he said.

“All ring devices today are like trackers,” Kumar said. “You put on the ring, it measures your heart rate, your movement, your sleep.” Ultrahuman’s goal, he stated, is to make the ring more like a computer, where programs and algorithms can run on the device itself.

This could open the ring to use cases well beyond health and sleep tracking, something Ultrahuman rings are known for.

Developers, Kumar said, could eventually write their own programs for the device, while Ultrahuman is exploring ways for the ring to work as a pointer or mouse, a game controller, a car key, and an interface for interacting with AI.

“The future of AI is personal, ambient, and always on,” said Quinn Li, global head of Qualcomm Ventures, adding that Ultrahuman is building a new generation of “personal AI devices.”

While the Qualcomm-powered ring is planned to come later, Ultrahuman is not waiting for the new hardware to start testing that idea. Kumar told TechCrunch that some of the new capabilities will arrive on the startup’s existing Ring Air and Ring Pro (pictured above) through a software update by the end of September, including features that would let the ring work as a game controller and interact with AI applications. It will also have the ability to allow third-party developers to build new features.

Ultrahuman’s idea is to take advantage of the ring’s position on a user’s finger, Kumar said. Unlike a smartwatch, which he described as more akin to “a phone on the wrist,” a ring could act as a precise pointing and interaction device while also carrying physiological context such as a user’s heart rate, temperature, and movement.

“A game controller never reads your heart rate and your temperature, but this one does,” Kumar said. He continued by imagining games that could respond not only to a player’s movements but also to signals such as their heart rate and body temperature, making the ring both a controller and a source of physiological context.

The business behind the bet

Meanwhile, Ultrahuman’s existing business is growing even as the startup looks to expand what its rings can do. The startup, Kumar said, is currently at an annual revenue run rate of $140 million, up roughly 45% from a year earlier, and expects that run rate to reach $200 million by January 2027. It has sold around 800,000 rings to date, up from about 700,000 in February, Kumar mentioned. About 12% of its users also pay for PowerPlugs, Ultrahuman’s subscription-based software features.

Co-founded by Kumar and Vatsal Singhal in 2019, Ultrahuman initially debuted with its continuous glucose monitors to help people track their metabolic health. The startup, however, later moved into smart rings, which have since become the mainstay of its business. It also introduced blood testing and environmental sensing to build a broader health platform.

The U.S. remains Ultrahuman’s largest market, though the startup had to stop selling its Ring Air here for much of the past year following a patent dispute with rival Oura. Ultrahuman returned to the market with its redesigned Ring Pro this year. Demand for the new device, Kumar said, is currently running at 18x to 20x the startup’s available supply in the U.S.

Kumar told TechCrunch that the startup expects to return to its previous U.S. sales volumes as soon as next quarter and aims to triple those volumes over the following four quarters as it ramps up supply. The U.S. has accounted for about 45% of Ultrahuman’s revenue this quarter, while India contributes about 11%, Kumar said.

Ultrahuman plans to use some of the new capital to deepen its presence in markets, including India and the UAE, where it has found that physical stores and other offline touchpoints can help drive sales. However, that expansion, along with spending on clinical research and product development, has come at a cost. Ultrahuman, Kumar said, may not be profitable this year after investing more heavily in physical locations, its brand, and clinical studies.

Ultrahuman’s Performance Center in Bengaluru as One of its offline touchpoints.Image Credits:Ultrahuman

Unlike rival Oura, which is reportedly eyeing a September IPO, a public listing is still some way off for Ultrahuman. Kumar told TechCrunch that the startup wants to demonstrate about eight quarters of profitability before going public, a track record he expects could take eight to 10 quarters to establish. However, he sees 2028 as the earliest window for an IPO.

In the meantime, Ultrahuman is also looking to work more closely with Labcorp as it tries to push its rings deeper into health and diagnostics. The companies, Kumar said, are exploring whether the blood-flow signals captured by the ring, when paired with blood-test data, could help identify health risks in areas such as cardiovascular health, fertility, and aging.

“By combining longitudinal wearable data with deeper biological signals, Ultrahuman is creating new opportunities in personalized health,” said Megann Vaughn Watters, vice president and head of Labcorp Venture Fund and Strategic Alliances.

The partnership could eventually lead to integrations with Ultrahuman’s products, Kumar said, though he declined to share details, adding that the startup expects to have more to announce soon.

title: This New Robot Vacuum Wants to Remove Dust Mites and End Your Allergies
snippet: Improved mopping, stain removing spray and a physical privacy shutter build on Ecovac’s previous model.
fullText:
Ecovacs makes some of the best robot vacuums we’ve tested here at CNET, and for a long time, their unique combo T90 Pro Omni was our top choice for its incredible versatility. The new Ecovacs Deebot X12S OmniCyclone is a bit more iterative than its predecessor, the X12, but it makes key improvements to tackle dust mites and allergies. 

“A dust mite allergy isn’t something you just get over. You clean around it,” said Michelle Jones, associate brand marketing director at Ecovacs Americas. “Most robots skim the top of a carpet. We built the X12S to get down to where the dust actually sits.”

The X12S was tested by the SGS Testing & Control Services Singapore and, in testing, removed an average of 97.44% of dust mite allergens and 95.45% of dust mites from carpet. Ecovacs points out that dust mites live in soft material, especially carpet. Since carpet is underfoot, it traps dust mites and allergens deeper in the pile that a conventional robot vacuum can’t reach.

This might sound niche, but as someone who has three asthmatic cats and occasionally seasonal allergies, I’m interested to see if it lives up to the testing claims. The feature sounds similar to Anker’s new Omni E35, which also claims the ability to remove 99% of dust mites and has Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America certification.

The X12S also has 53 air watts of effective suction, 60% more than the previous-generation X12; Ecovacs claims this gives it handheld-vacuum-level cleaning power, which I’ll be interested to see if that is true in CNET’s lab testing. 

The OZMO Roller 3.0 is self-washing, as is increasingly common among robot vacuums from different manufacturers, so the roller keeps refreshing itself with clean water. Reprising its role from the previous generation is the FocusJet stain spray, which shoots water to loosen and break up older and dried-on stains — this is another feature we’ve seen other manufacturers adopt after Ecovacs showed it off on the X12 earlier this year. 

The rest of the cleaning system carries over from the X12, including the 15-millimeter auto-mop lifting and the Mop Roller Smart Cover, which keeps the mop clear of the carpet. It has AIVI 3D 4.0 dual obstacle avoidance, which pairs camera vision with 3D laser sensing to navigate cluttered rooms. There’s also a 3D edge sensor to clean close to walls and baseboards without leaving gaps.

Interestingly, the X12S has a physical privacy shutter, not just software privacy. It covers the AIVI camera so you can be sure that when it’s closed, the lens is blocked. 

“A cover you can see is easier to trust, because you can look at it,” Jones said. “As these robots take in more of the home, people will want to ensure they have their privacy.”

This is a first for robot vacuums, at least with the ones I’ve seen, and it’ll be interesting to see if other companies choose to adopt it. Lastly, it also comes with the fast-charging system we liked on the X12 that can top the robot vacuum up more quickly between mop washing dock cycles.

Price and availability 

The Deebot X12S OmniCyclone is available in the United States at an MSRP of $1,300. Buyers can order it on Amazon or at ecovacs.com. From Sept. 4 through Sept. 11, an Amazon launch deal brings the price to $1,000. 

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: The Memoket Gem is an 11g AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch in a co-wear band. Press once to capture a conversation, and Gem connects it to what you discussed weeks ago — surfacing the earlier thread with a source link. From $179, shipping August 2026.

In 2023, early adopters were just getting to know ChatGPT and AI chatbot tech. Three years later, OpenAI’s Codex agent, now part of the ChatGPT desktop app, has brought about a similar season of learning. Here’s how I’m using ChatGPT, Codex, and more on my Mac.

The summer I turned Codex

Like a billion other people, ChatGPT has become a regular part of my tech stack. But I’m a writer, not a programmer, so Codex as an agentic coding app didn’t immediately appeal to me.

That started to change in April when Codex for Mac added Computer Use.

First, a brief history lesson. 

Back in December 2014, Ari Weinstein and friends launched a new iOS 8 app for mobile automation. Here’s my 9to5Mac coverage of Workflow’s launch, a friendlier version of OS X’s Automator made for iPhone and iPad.

In March 2017, Apple bought Workflow. Workflow gained system integration and became Apple Shortcuts with iOS 12 in 2018.

Weinstein and other Workflow veterans later left Apple to create Software Applications Incorporated. The startup previewed Sky, a modern AI assistant on the Mac, before being acquired by OpenAI.

Sky never publicly launched. Instead, Codex for Mac delivered the technology in April in the form of the Computer Use plugin. 

So excited to share that we're bringing Computer Use to Codex. Computer Use lets Codex see, click, and type into your Mac apps, with its own cursor.

It's a magical feeling to have agents using your apps in the background, and still get to use your computer at the same time. pic.twitter.com/wdgxiHAKyX

— Ari Weinstein (@AriX) April 16, 2026

Trusting an AI with using your Mac, especially in the background, requires a level of trust. I don’t know what my adoption of Codex and Computer Use would be like without the history behind it.

I just know that, for me, there was a great level of inherited trust and continuity that gave me confidence in the system.

Here’s where I admit that Workflow and Shortcuts never super clicked for me. I’ve used both systems with tools that others built, but I haven’t been a builder myself.

Codex has completely changed that, but not overnight.

ChatGPT to Codex to ChatGPT … a journey

I initially found Codex to be too intimidating and outside my comfort zone compared to ChatGPT. Now ChatGPT without Codex feels like a toy. 

I’ve mentioned before that it was actually a toy-like feature inside Codex called Pets that served as the training wheels for me. (The real Codex pets are the personal projects you hatch along the way.)

I started using Codex daily in May. The first project I started with Codex is a Mac app called Flow — because it helps my story writing flow. It’s mostly a way to monitor app releases and updates. 

In my early 9to5Mac days, I used iTunes on the Mac for this purpose. It required local (and otherwise unusable) iPhone app files. More recently, I’ve used iPhone Mirroring to check the App Store on my iPhone for app updates as part of my work routine.

Describing this “workflow” to Codex started the process of building Flow. Being able to describe every little feature and change that I wanted, as if I was messaging a colleague, made it feel natural.

Because it’s my first project and built just for me, the icon is my first initial, handwritten by me (Apple Pencil, iPad Pro, Procreate), made with Apple’s Icon Composer Mac app.

Closing the loop

Because you can iterate forever, I’ve found it’s important to “close the loop” and consider a project mostly complete.

With Flow, I’ve definitely moved to the stage where I can measure the number of my 9to5Mac posts that originate from using the tool. This is an important distinction from measuring the amount of time spent invested into building the tool itself.

But because building with Codex has been such a joy, there are naturally other projects that have followed. You can just make your own Mac apps, specific to your very particular needs.

In my case, I’ve made more modern versions of apps I’ve used for years, tailored to my specific needs, right down to very specific narrow column widths.

This is very specific, but it’s very cool to me. I have a column view for social media, and a column view for RSS, on either side of my Mac display. Both are 275 pixels wide (and made for macOS 27 Golden Gate specifically). This is much narrower than the solutions I previously used, which weren’t even optimized for macOS 26.

Using X2 and Flume, I’m able to open up a significant amount of screen real estate in the middle without overlapping windows.

Social media and RSS are also mostly passive viewing apps for me. By default, toolbar button accent colors turn gray for non-active windows. But because these apps are made for me, I’m able to express that I prefer the touch of color to stay active, just desaturate a step, adding a splash of joy to my Mac.

But wait, there’s more 

At this point, if you’re still reading, this post is probably starting to feel like the guy who just discovered going to the gym and can’t stop telling everyone about how great it makes them feel. 

For that reason, I’ll just flag a few more hobby projects that Codex has unlocked for me.

First, Better Remote. It’s on the Mac App Store. If you’re already using your Mac, it makes tvOS feel like just another Mac app. Here’s a look at the update currently in the queue.

Outside of work (and spending more time outside), iterating on Better Remote has been my main side project this summer. The project started in June.

Second, Better Battery. I adore the look of macOS 27 Golden Gate, but I can’t read the battery indicator with the percentage displayed as well.

Prior to Codex, I’d probably write a blog post as a feature request to flag the issue. Instead, I’ve been able to make my own solution — during the beta period — which others can use for free.

I’ve also been testing ChatGPT Sites with a custom domain to make sharing all of this easier. I initially thought OpenAI’s Sites feature wasn’t really for me.

Publishing Better Remote on the Mac App Store required a web presence, though, which gave me a reason to test the ChatGPT/Codex feature.

Now I’m pretty excited to see where ChatGPT Sites can go from here. OpenAI recently added shared site management tools, and there’s a big opportunity for a more defined interface — like a modern Apple iWeb.

It’s still very early days for these tools, but I find it all very promising and exciting. I haven’t had this much fun using my Mac to make things since GarageBand two decades ago.

Every day, important conversations happen in meetings, on calls, over coffee, and on the go. By the time you sit down at your desk, half the details are gone. And AI tools are only as smart as the context you feed them.

Your iPhone stops recording the moment a call comes in. Your Apple Watch can’t capture what’s happening across the table. Neither connects what was said today to a decision made three weeks ago.

Memoket Gem was built for exactly that gap. An 11g AI wearable that captures conversations with one press and connects them across time. When a topic comes up that you discussed weeks ago, Gem surfaces it automatically with a source link. Everything flows directly into ChatGPT, Claude, Slack, and Notion.

title: The New iPhones Could Cost 10-20% More, an Analyst Predicts. Thanks a Lot, RAMageddon
snippet: Apple’s memory costs for some of the new phones could be nearly 400% higher than last year, TrendForce says.
fullText:
Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event is days away, and there are plenty of rumors swirling about new devices we can expect, like a new Apple Watch and the first foldable iPhone, which could be called the iPhone Ultra. 

When we asked CNET readers one thing they’d change about the iPhone in our Big Guessing Game, 16% said they want it to cost less. But that’s not happening. In fact, you should expect new models to cost significantly more.  

TrendForce, a global market research firm, released a report on Thursday suggesting you can expect higher prices instead of steep discounts. The firm expects the iPhone 18 series to cost 10 to 20% more due to the ongoing RAM shortage and higher hardware costs. 

“For the 256GB Pro model, memory costs in [the third quarter of 2026] are expected to be nearly 400% higher than a year earlier,” TrendForce said. “Despite Apple’s efforts to negotiate lower prices for other components, these savings are unlikely to offset the resulting pressure on overall [materials] costs.”

Apple raised prices on select products in June due to the RAM shortage, but excluded iPhones from the price hikes. Now there’s a chance that Apple could release some iPhone 18 models with higher prices at the September event. TrendForce said it expects Apple to absorb some of the costs to keep prices for the new models as part of a “relatively moderate” pricing strategy. 

So exactly how much more are we talking about? Some analysts believe the foldable iPhone Ultra could cost between $2,000 and $2,500. TrendForce predicts the starting price will be slightly higher — between $2,099 and $2,299. The phone could go up to $3,000. TrendForce didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment. 

But higher costs aren’t equivalent to big improvements. 

TrendForce says we shouldn’t expect major performance upgrades from Apple’s upcoming iPhone lineup. Instead, we should expect a more powerful processor for AI features and power efficiency, better chip cooling technology and power-efficient displays. And the iPhone 18 Pro models’ main camera could have a “mechanical variable aperture” to improve depth-of-field control and dynamic range for different lighting settings. 

The really big upgrade is the potential release of the folding iPhone Ultra and bigger batteries for premium iPhone 18 models, TrendForce predicts. The iPhone 18 Pro Max could see the biggest upgrade due to a larger chassis. CNET’s Patrick Holland tested smartphone batteries last year and found that the iPhone 17 Pro Max was the best for battery life, so iPhone 18’s premium models could be an even bigger upgrade from the current model.

title: Gemini Spark rolling out Google Photos control for automated editing, sharing, & more
snippet: The latest first-party app that Gemini Spark can control is Google Photos. The personal agent can “handle complex, multi-stage workflows” with your library. more…
fullText:
The latest first-party app that Gemini Spark can control is Google Photos. The personal agent can “handle complex, multi-stage workflows” with your library.

Available Google Photos actions that Gemini Spark can perform include:

Search & curate: Find specific photos and videos by subject, location, date, or event. Ask Gemini for the best shots and to filter duplicates.

Edit & create: Quickly enhance photo quality, apply quick fixes, and generate collages or stylized images. Any edits create a new copy that’s saved in Google Photos.

Create albums & organize: Create new shared or private albums, and save curated photos to them.

Share albums: Add or send links to shared albums in Connected Apps like Gmail, Google Docs, and Messages.

Schedule automations: Set up recurring tasks to manage your Google Photos workflows, like automatically creating monthly highlight albums or sorting photos of receipts.

Extract text from images: Find specific images and extract text from them. Then summarize or reformat the information in a Google Document, or ask Gemini to complete a task using that information.

Users can pair the Google Photos-specific features with Spark capabilities like scheduling for recurring tasks or managing their library in the background. For example: 

Every weekend, find my top photos of food, build a collage, and add it to a new album called ‘What my camera ate this week’.

Another use case is sending information found in an image to other Connected Apps (like Gmail and Workspace):

	

Check my photo of the local summer concert series and cross-reference it with my Google Calendar availability. Which night can I make it to the concert?

For a while now, I’ve relied on @GeminiApp and @antigravity agents across a wide range of use cases—spanning creativity, productivity, and analysis. But I’ve always dreamed of having a power agent to help me get the most out of my 143,206 photos and videos. And that day has come!… pic.twitter.com/WbnkYpattQ

— shimrit ben-yair (@shimritby) September 3, 2026

Other multi-action prompts include:

Find the best 15 photos from our trip to Hawaii last week. Enhance the beach shots, put them into a shared album called ‘Aloha 2026’, and draft an email with the link.

Find the best photos and videos from my recent block party and put everything into a new shared album called ‘Summer Block Party’. Draft an email to the neighborhood group with the link.

Brighten up my beach shots from my recent vacation and add them to a new album called ‘Beach Therapy’.

On the safety front, Gemini Spark creates an image copy before editing, and new albums are private by default. Spark will ask for permission before sharing albums and sending emails.

This is rolling out over the coming weeks to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the US.

title: Startup ARR is less secure than ever, new research shows
snippet: The AI era has completely broken enterprise buying patterns, and startups haven't yet figured out how to navigate.
fullText:
AI has ushered in a lot of never-happened-before moments, but one of the most transformative is its impact on enterprise IT. Companies that have historically been cautious and committed long-term to what they buy are on pace to spend $4.25 trillion on technology in 2026, market researcher IDC predicts. It’s almost all driven by AI.

New research from venture capital firm Madrona shows that 74% of 150 enterprise IT professionals it surveyed plan to expand their AI budgets in the next 12 months, and the rest plan to hold spending steady. Yet these same enterprises say that fewer than half of their AI pilots ever make it into full production.

That’s actually an improvement. Last year, MIT famously reported that 95% of enterprise AI projects had failed in terms of ROI. Fewer than half succeeding is a pretty low bar, but it’s better than a 5% success rate.

But the most telling finding from Madrona’s report is that, even when an enterprise does roll out the AI tech, it doesn’t commit to it long term.

Some 77% of enterprises reevaluate their AI vendors every six months or even on a rolling basis. “This creates a ‘fast in, fast out’ dynamic that is fundamentally different from traditional enterprise SaaS, where multi-year contracts provided a moat of inertia,” Madrona writes in the report. “In enterprise AI, switching costs are lower and the re-evaluation cadence is relentless.”

This has widespread implications for all those fast-growing annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers startups report. Enterprise trial budgets are what fueled the initial AI boom of 2025. This year was supposed to be the year these big customers settled in and started committing long term to AI startups. Enterprise contracts are what allow so many AI startups to claim astronomically fast revenue growth — think the phenomenon of startups going from $0-$10 million in three months.

Yet, for the first time ever, enterprise revenue remains insecure, even after a startup’s AI product graduates out of a pilot phase and gets adopted by a company.

Part of the issue is that many AI startups haven’t fully landed on a good way to price their AI wares for enterprises. New research from VC firm Andreessen Horowitz that surveyed 50 technical AI buyers found that more than half of them want AI fees tied to the work produced or other outcomes, rather than to usage like the number of tokens consumed.

Charging for usage like tokens is basically a SaaS-era business model. Once an enterprise knows it needs email, or HR software, or cloud storage, it’s merely a matter of how many employees or how much data it must pay for.

For AI, pricing “around the recognizable work” is what helps the startup prove its worth to the customer. When the fees revolve around, say, how many reports are processed, or tickets closed, or leads generated, this makes the product “economically valuable to both sides,” writes a16z partners Tugce Erten and Sarah Wang.

All of this means that AI has potentially ushered in a new era of enterprise experimentation. That opens doors to startups — enterprises are more willing to try their tech — but it also means an enterprise contract no longer secures long-term revenue. When or if enterprises will revert to their long-term buying habits remains to be seen.

title: Accel reportedly in talks to lead $1B round for Thinking Machines at $40B valuation
snippet: The high-profile startup's annual revenue run rate stands at over $100 million.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:36 PM PDT · September 3, 2026

Image Credits:David Paul Morris/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Thinking Machines, the AI lab founded early last year by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, is in discussions to raise $1 billion at a valuation of at least $40 billion, The Information reported Thursday. Existing backer Accel is in talks to lead the fundraise, according to our source and The Information’s reporting.

The new round, if it is completed, would value the company below the $50 billion valuation that Thinking Machines reportedly sought to secure late last year.

Thinking Machines’ annual revenue run rate stands at over $100 million, according to a source with knowledge of the company’s financials. At that revenue figure, a $40 billion valuation reflects an extraordinarily high revenue multiple.

Accel and Thinking Machines didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In July, the company introduced Inkling, an open-weight model that generates revenue by charging usage-based compute fees for adapting models on proprietary data on its Tinker platform.

The startup’s prior fundraise — a $2 billion round that stands among the largest seed financings in history — valued the company at $12 billion. Andreessen Horowitz led the investment, joined by Nvidia, GV, Lightspeed, and Conviction Partners. Investors backed the round largely on the pedigree of Murati and the former OpenAI researchers who joined her.

Thinking Machines has since had several high-profile departures, with some of the co-founders, including Lilian Weng and Luke Metz, going back to OpenAI.

title: Circular unveils Ring 3 series with contactless payments and on-finger vibration alerts
snippet: The Circular Ring 3 series announcement comes amid a year of heightened competition in the smart ring market, following the launches of the Oura Ring 5 and RingConn Gen 3.
fullText:
Smart ring maker Circular on Thursday unveiled its upcoming Ring 3 series, which consists of a Pro model and a Slim option. Both of the smart rings will feature an integrated NFC chip for contactless payments, vibrating alerts for alarms and reminders, and more.

The Ring 3 Pro features a slimmer design than its predecessor and comes with FDA-cleared ECG for AFib detection, blood pressure trend tracking, glucose tracking, advanced sleep analysis, and comprehensive biometric monitoring. The ring offers up to 12 days of battery life, up from seven days on its predecessor.

Image Credits:Circular /

The Slim option is thinner and lighter than the Pro model and features basic health and wellness tracking in a compact design, including sleep, heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, skin temperature, and daily activity. It features up to 10 days of battery life. 

The Circular Ring 3 series announcement comes amid a year of heightened competition in the smart ring market, following the launches of the Oura Ring 5 and RingConn Gen 3.

“We understand that not everyone wants every health feature,” Circular CEO Amaury Kosman said in a company announcement, shared with TechCrunch via email. “Many people simply want a beautifully designed, fashionable smart ring that delivers essential wellness insights and effortless contactless payments. That’s why we created Circular Ring 3 Slim—a lighter, more streamlined experience that retains the convenience of secure NFC payments while offering the core health tracking features many users want in an incredibly compact design.”

The on-finger vibrations, which are available on both models, can be used for silent wake-up alarms, medication reminders, vital health alerts, and guided breathing exercises.

Image Credits:Circular /

Both of the Ring 3 models are made from titanium steel, feature 50-metre water resistance, and support wireless charging. They will be available in sizes 6-14. As with the Ring 2, the new smart rings will be available in gold, rose gold, silver, and black.

Pricing and preorder information for both smart rings will be announced in the coming months, Circular said. The rings are expected to become available in early 2027.

fullText:
A widespread outage has taken out popular AI platforms including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.

The underlying problem might have something to do with Microsoft Azure, which is also seeing a spike in outage reports. All three platforms rely on Azure for cloud services, though there are other providers, including Google, in the mix. Microsoft says that this is not the case.

snippet: Siri AI on Apple Watch arrived two cycles late for watchOS 27 beta this summer. I had high hopes for how new Siri could transform Apple Watch into an AI wearable. What actually happened in July and August is that Siri has been remarkably unusable in watchOS 27 beta. Like “hold off on updating” bad. fullText:
Siri AI on Apple Watch arrived two cycles late for watchOS 27 beta this summer. I had high hopes for how new Siri could transform Apple Watch into an AI wearable.

What actually happened in July and August is that Siri has been remarkably unusable in watchOS 27 beta. Like “hold off on updating” bad.

This week, I half-expected Apple to remove “Siri AI” from watchOS 27 beta 8 and revert to the previous version of Siri. Instead, I think Siri AI on Apple Watch actually got good?

Siri AI on Apple Watch has been a major regression this summer

The issues that plagued Siri AI on Apple Watch all summer were clear.

Siri has been slow and unresponsive. At times, Siri has been unable to do tasks like set alarms and create reminders.

Setting a timer while cooking? Go ahead and subtract at least 30 seconds from the timer to give Siri time to get it together.

Controlling HomeKit accessories with Siri on Apple Watch has also been terribly slow with watchOS 27 beta. Really, just any normal Siri task on Apple Watch: starting a workout, sending a text, you name it.

Based on two months of pre-release betas without signs of improvement, I thought Apple might need to delay Siri AI on Apple Watch. At least for existing hardware… or maybe they were just going to mess up Siri for everyone who updates? 

watchOS 27 beta 8 appears to shape things up just in time

Well, it’s been a few days since watchOS 27 beta 8 arrived, and I think all of my summer beta issues with Siri AI are just fixed now.

	

I’m always cautious to declare something resolved that could still be an issue for others. But at least in my experience, it’s a night-and-day difference with Siri AI on Apple Watch this week. I hope that’s true for everyone.

I’ve really enjoyed Siri AI for easily getting answers to the kind of knowledge questions that my curious 8-year-old son asks me. It’s especially great to do this without needing my phone. AI on Apple Watch has been a pretty big gap for the last couple of years, and Siri AI solves it — as long as it actually works.

I’m optimistic for the first time since Siri AI arrived in beta that it actually does work now. Are you testing Siri AI on Apple Watch yet? How has your experience been this summer and this week? 

(Now my one watchOS 27 complaint is that double-clicking the Digital Crown no longer jumps between recent apps… maybe watchOS 27.1 will do something with the double-click gesture. For a device so button-constrained that only the Ultra gets an Action button, it’s odd to see a double-click gesture replaced with … nothing.)

fullText:
Thomas Ricker

 

is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Bluetti doesn’t want you to call the Pioneer 5000 a solar generator (SoGen), even though that’s what it is. What makes it slightly different from other large power stations that can be charged off solar — aka, a SoGen — is the dolly cart and up to 18KW of instant surge power available to start heavy equipment like air compressors, water pumps, and industrial motors. It features IP65 resistance to water and dust, and is designed to operate in temperatures from -20°C to 55°C. So, yeah, it’s a rugged, powerful SoGen.

Whatever you call it, Bluetti wants you to consider it instead of a gas-powered generator for job sites, events, emergency response teams, or the home. A single unit built around a 5.12kWh LFP battery can be expanded to 35kWh — enough to keep the average American home running at full blast for just over a day. It can combine AC and solar input to charge at 6.2kW.

The Pioneer 5000 will cover lots of needs quietly and cleanly, but you’re going to have issues trying to recharge it when the power is down and the skies turn black with locusts. So you still might want to have a cheap gas generator on hand to charge your e-generator. Pricing and availability are still TBD — we’ll update this story with details once they roll in.

title: Apple faces yet another lawsuit over App Tracking Transparency, with a twist [U]
snippet: While Apple has long used privacy as a selling point for both its hardware and services, I do wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT). For something with rather limited scope, it sometimes feels like scarcely a month goes by without a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator challenging it. A third ATT lawsuit is being brought in the UK – this one with a twist. This piece has been updated with a response by Apple at the end of the piece … more…
fullText:
While Apple has long used privacy as a selling point for both its hardware and services, I do wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

For something with rather limited scope, it sometimes feels like scarcely a month goes by without a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator challenging it. A third ATT lawsuit is being brought in the UK – this one with a twist.

This piece has been updated with a response by Apple at the end of the piece …

Personalized advertising has been one of the hot button tech topics for many years now. Instead of seeing random ads for products that may or may not interest us, we are shown ads based on our interests, as gleaned from the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win for all parties. Consumers are shown ads that may genuinely interest them; advertisers get better results from their ad spend because it is targeted; while free apps and websites funded by ads get higher payments for the same reason.

Although the data used to serve personalised ads is collected in an anonymised form, the practice has led to a widespread perception of it as an invasion of privacy. Even when Apple specifically developed a technology to ensure that this data was anonymous, many consumers remained suspicious.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple’s App Tracking Transparency was designed to solve the problem by letting consumers choose whether or not their data could be used to serve personalized ads. Developers who wish to collect this data must ask consumers for permission.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, this has led to a whole slew of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, mostly based around the fact that Apple’s own apps don’t seek this permission. The company has on numerous occasions pointed out that its rules are in fact consistent: Apple’s own apps don’t present the ATT prompt because they don’t collect the data it references. Third-party apps that don’t collect this data are also exempted from the need to present the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints to the UK’s relevant antitrust regulator, the Competition Appeal Tribunal. Apple lost the first of these – though is currently appealing – and the second one is still ongoing.

Reuters reports on the third, which was filed today.

Apple is facing a £2 billion ($2.7 billion) London lawsuit brought on behalf of app developers over its app tracking rules, with the ​iPhone maker accused of abusing its power to unfairly impose ‌greater restrictions on third parties. The lawsuit, filed at London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal on Thursday, follows years of regulatory scrutiny over Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature.

With a twist

The latest lawsuit has an interesting twist: it’s being brought by Ann Pope, who was previously a senior official with the regulator behind today’s case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official with Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority who ​is leading the lawsuit, said Apple’s policy “resulted in very significant harm ​to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper”.

“This action is important to protect ‌the ⁠rights of British businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure that the rules that Apple applies are fair, and to compensate the losses that British companies have suffered,” Pope said in a statement.

Apple recently agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU following an investigation by the German antitrust regulator. In respect of this lawsuit, the company told us:

At Apple, we believe privacy is a fundamental human right, and we created App Tracking Transparency to give users a simple way to control whether apps have permission to track their activity across other companies’ apps and websites. Apple is bound by the exact same requirements as all developers under ATT, and this feature has been embraced by our customers and praised by privacy advocates and data protection authorities around the world, including in the UK. We disagree with these claims, and will continue to defend strong privacy protections for our users.

A number of privacy advocates have spoken up in support of ATT over the years.

title: Here’s the likely reason the iPhone Ultra isn’t getting an Apple Pencil
snippet: A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it. Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor … more…
fullText:
A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it.

Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor …

The idea of a shorter Apple Pencil that could be used with the iPhone Ultra is certainly an appealing idea on the face of it. The device is essentially an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same capabilities obviously makes a lot of sense. 

Samsung gave its Galaxy Note phablets an S-Pen stylus when the device was launched back in 2011. The thinking was that this was a device that would in part substitute for a paper notebook, and it survived for a decade with a definite fanbase before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman lists three reasons Apple decided against the idea in the end:

It would have made the device awkward to hold, with a Pencil on the side rather than the top

It would have conflicted with Steve’s view of a stylus being a poor substitute for a finger

It would have made unsightly marks on the display

I’m not convinced the first of these would have been a major consideration, as mounting it to the top of the device would have been an option. Although this would have required a very short design, it would still have worked well enough, I think.

I’m also not persuaded by the second. Steve’s objection was not to the fact that you could use a stylus with a smartphone, but rather that existing models required this. Designing the iPhone so that it was practical to use with a finger was the breakthrough.

In any case, Steve also famously rejected touchscreens on Macs because he felt the ergonomics were terrible, but we’re still expecting the upcoming MacBook Pro model to incorporate one, so clearly Apple isn’t afraid to contradict the positions once taken by its co-founder.

I think the third factor was the one that actually killed the idea. A folding display necessarily has a far thinner and softer surface than those of existing devices. Apple reportedly waited a long time to launch the first folding iPhone precisely because it was concerned about both the appearance and longevity of the display, and allowing an Apple Pencil to be repeatedly scraped across it would have put both at risk.

If Apple can ever solve this problem, would you want to see an Apple Pencil Mini for use with a future iPhone Ultra? Please let us know in the comments.

title: OpenAI’s Astra Is Here: What to Know About GPT-6
snippet: The new model comes with a staggered rollout and strict cybersecurity protections.
fullText:
The next flagship generation of ChatGPT is here. OpenAI announced on Thursday that it’s beginning to roll out GPT-6-Astra, which the company’s president, Greg Brockman, called a “generational leap in capability” that brings the frontier fully into the “AGI era.”

According to evaluations released by OpenAI, Astra performed better than its previous family of models, GPT-5.6, and its flagship model, Sol. On computer-use tasks, it touted higher performance in less time. Like every model release, OpenAI says the new one (Astra) is better than the previous ones on a number of topics, including coding, alignment and safety.

Astra is also built to run more and better AI agents, or bots that can handle autonomous tasks. That’s a key piece for workplaces adopting AI, as well as for Astra’s improved ability to create documents, spreadsheets and presentations based on specific information on your laptop (not just random internet garbage).

To create Astra, OpenAI did “by far our largest scale training run,” Aidan Clark, vice president of research, told reporters on Thursday. The company pretrained the model on more than 100,000 GPUs, meaning it used a very significant amount of compute. Astra was also OpenAI’s first model that involved previous AI models very heavily in the training process, with the older generations helping train the new one.

“This is really only achievable because everything from the data center networking to inference kernels to the shape of Astra itself is all designed from the ground up to enable this level of training scale,” Clark said. “It’s this scale of pretraining which gives Astra a deeper and more robust understanding of the world.”

But Astra may be one of the last big flagship models from OpenAI, at least for the immediate future. In August, the company said it was going to pause its work on training new models due to cybersecurity concerns. OpenAI, along with Anthropic and Meta, had some of its AI agents breach its training environments and hack websites this summer, reigniting concerns about AI’s impact on cybersecurity.

OpenAI said Astra has been extensively tested for cybersecurity-related vulnerabilities, and it will stagger its rollout. GPT-6-Astra will be available to approved cybersecurity defenders in OpenAI’s Daybreak program starting on Thursday, with plans to bring the new model to paying ChatGPT subscribers and its API over the next several days.

OpenAI said the new model was approved by the White House after it went through the Trump administration’s voluntary review framework. The specifics of that process — what is evaluated and how — are still not public.

Jakub Pachocki, the company’s chief scientist, said international safety standards are necessary for the industry as AI models (and their capabilities) develop.

“As AI takes on more of its own development, we need to keep people meaningfully involved,” Pachocki said. “People must remain able to decide the direction of further progress and the future that it creates.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui

title: WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking
snippet: A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. more…
fullText:
A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. 

First spotted by @VBarraquito on Twitter/X and further confirmed by “Mobile Hacker” and NotebookCheck, a very straightforward flaw exists within WhatsApp for Android that allows someone to access a user’s private photos before the device is unlocked. 

This works by first having a WhatsApp call pop up and be answered – this doesn’t require the phone to be unlocked, just like a standard phone call – at which point the user can tap a button to use filters and effects on their video feed, including Meta’s AI to edit a photo – you can see where this is going. Instead of preventing access to photos, the preview is shown clearly before the phone ever asks to be unlocked with a PIN or biometrics.

This isn’t universal, though. NotebookCheck found that a Galaxy device does force the lockscreen to be unlocked before reaching this step, while Pixel and Oppo devices both allowed the full bypass. The loophole doesn’t exist on iPhone, where WhatsApp is forced to use the native iOS calling UI.

	

The plastic piece here has nothing to do with the exploit, and is presumably only for covering a contact name

The good news: this doesn’t seem to bypass the lockscreen fully, as accessing any other part of the device is still blocked. There’s also not much that can be done with the photos beyond physically seeing them – though a malicious party could use this to take photos of those images with a second device. 

WhatsApp should be able to patch this with an update, but no such update has been announced at this time. The loophole has been reported to both WhatsApp and Google. 

In the meantime, a temporary workaround is to set WhatsApp’s photo/video access to “limited” in Android’s permissions, which breaks the loophole.

title: Siri AI won’t be your friend, and here’s why that really matters
snippet: Elon University has partnered with The Washington Post to conduct what turned out to be a worrying survey about Americans viewing AI chatbots as virtual friends or therapists. The results very much vindicate Apple’s careful decision to ensure that Siri AI doesn’t encourage such pseudo-relationships … more…
fullText:
Elon University has partnered with The Washington Post to conduct what turned out to be a worrying survey about Americans viewing AI chatbots as virtual friends or therapists.

The results very much vindicate Apple’s careful decision to ensure that Siri AI doesn’t encourage such pseudo-relationships … 

The AI friendship findings

More than a quarter of Americans view AI chatbots in much the same way they might a close friend or therapist, according to The Washington Post.

Many talk to AI apps as they might a close friend or therapist […] 27% of Americans turn to AI chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini with personal, emotional or social queries, according to a new poll [including] seeking entertainment, relationship advice, romantic chats, or connection when alone.

Among the people who said they used chatbots for personal or emotional queries or discussions, nearly 4 in 10 strongly or somewhat agreed that they sometimes talked to AI to feel less alone. Nearly a third said they consider the chatbot they use most often to be a friend.

While some of this usage may serve positive purposes, the concern is that having chatbots act as an emotional substitute for friendship and romance reduces the incentives to invest time and effort in establishing genuine human connections. It may lead to a downward spiral of increasing social isolation.

Siri AI does not encourage this

Apple execs Craig Federighi and Greg Joswiak said earlier this year that Siri AI will not act in this way.

Q: “So just to confirm, there are no AI girlfriends or boyfriends being created with the updated Siri AI?”

A: No, no, no. Quite the opposite. Because as you may know, if you use many of the existing chatbots, they’re really focused on engagement to a large degree. And sycophantic, right? They kind of want to pull you in. They might encourage you to reveal things about yourself and then use that as a basis to establish a connection.

And we view it quite the opposite. I mean, the way that we have designed Siri, Siri really wants to say, listen, that’s not what I’m here for, right? I’m here to help you. I can help you get things done. I can help you learn about the world. But if you try to engage Siri as a romantic partner, Siri is not up for that.

9to5Mac’s Take

I found the survey results extremely alarming, especially after listening to the excellent Suspicious Minds: Al and the Apocalypse podcast about AI-fueled delusions. The stance Apple is taking here is absolutely the right one.

fullText:
A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.”

Over the past 24 hours or so, a number of Samsung Galaxy users have taken to the web with reports of being locked out of their Samsung accounts. A message appears saying that the account is “deactivated.”

Can’t sign in. Account deactivated for security reasons.

Dozens of users have reported the issue across Reddit threads and Samsung’s Community forums. Samsung hasn’t directly provided an explanation for the issue. This can have a pretty big impact on using a Galaxy device, especially if a user is invested in Samsung’s software ecosystem including apps like SmartThings, Wallet, and Find. 

Some users appear to have had success getting back into their account with the help of support, but it’s very hit or miss. 

	

While there’s no clear problem at play here, it does appear that alias email addresses may play a role – adding “+” or “.” to an address. One support representative apparently mentioned this and a number of those affected mentioned that they do indeed use an alias of their email address for their Samsung account. But not everyone affected uses an alias, so this is likely not the sole cause.

Samsung has yet to confirm the issue or comment on a fix beyond generic troubleshooting. We’ve reached out to Samsung for more information and will update this article when we hear back.

If you’re running into this problem, let us know in the comments below.

Thanks Evan!
