title: Apple Card keeps getting better, here’s everything new
snippet: Apple Card launched seven years ago this month, and it keeps getting better. There are new features, perks, rewards, and more. Plus, there’s one major change looming. Here’s everything new with Apple Card lately. more…
fullText:
Apple Card launched seven years ago this month, and it keeps getting better. There are new features, perks, rewards, and more. Plus, there’s one major change looming.

Here’s everything new with Apple Card lately.

iOS 27: Recurring transactions

As my colleague Ryan highlighted last month, iOS 27 adds a really useful new “Recurring” feature to the Wallet app for Apple Card. You can find the “Recurring” hub by tapping the three-dot menu in the top-right corner.

In this menu, you’ll see a list of upcoming recurring transactions that are set to be charged to your Apple Card. This includes the date and the amount of the expected transaction. In addition to viewing the transactions as a list, you can also see them on a monthly calendar view.

It’s a helpful new feature for Apple Card users in iOS 27. The update is currently available to public beta testers and developers, and will likely be released to everyone next month.

New status perk

Earlier this month, Apple added a new perk for Apple Card users who travel a lot.

Apple has teamed up with Booking.com to offer all Apple Card users “Genius Level 2” status after one stay or car rental. You also get 3% Daily Cash on all Booking.com transactions.

What do you get with “Genius Level 2” status? Apple says your status could “unlock benefits on select stays and car rentals such as 10–15% discounts, free breakfast and room upgrades.”

Hertz partnership

Last year, Apple announced a partnership with Hertz to provide exclusive perks when you book a caar rental with your Apple Card:

Free Emergency Roadside Service

Add loss damage waiver vehicle protection for the discounted rate of $16.95 per day (plus tax).

Add a free additional driver at pickup.

Save at least 5% off Pay Later base rates.

Additionally, Apple Card offers 3% Daily Cash for car rentals booked through Hertz.

Apple Card Savings Account expansion

One criticism people have of Apple Card is that it relies on your iPhone for key account management features. Since the Apple Card launch, Apple has worked to improve that.

Most recently, Apple launched web access for Apple Card Savings. This means you can now view and manage your Apple Card Savings Account directly in your web browser.

A big change looms

The big change hanging over Apple Card right now, however, is its impending move from Goldman Sachs to Chase. Apple announced the deal back in January and said the transition will occur “in approximately 24 months.”

Many questions remain about what Apple Card’s future looks like under Chase. Apple has promised that several key things about Apple Card won’t change under Chase’s leadership. We should learn more concrete details over the next 18 months as Chase, Goldman Sachs, and Apple iron out the details behind the scenes.

Wrap up

Are you an Apple Card cardholder? What do you think about it? Personally, I think it’s an excellent option for people in the Apple ecosystem, even if you can usually find better rewards through other ecosystems. I use my Apple Card to pay for my Apple subscriptions to get 3% Daily Cash back. The option to finance Apple hardware purchases with 0% interest is also very compelling.

Let me know what you think down in the comments.

title: Dyson’s Huge Pipe-like Air Purifier Moves Like a Dune Sandworm and Blows Air Across the Room
snippet: These combo models can heat, cool and clean air all in the same unit.
fullText:
Dyson’s HushJet air purifiers have been some of the versatile air purifiers on the market, able to cool, purify and heat the air, so you get climate control capabilities in addition to purification. The new HushJet purifier range, announced at the IFA 2026 trade show in Berlin, incorporates all of these capabilities with a complete redesign and I was able to see all three models in person prior to the show.

The new HushJet models look like large curved pipes, a design Dyson calls the “HushJet Nozzle.” It incorporates the directed-fan capabilities of the HushJet MiniCool Fan that we loved for portable summer cooling, with the aerospace turbine design of the HushJet Compact, for more consistent performance and reduced noise and turbulence.

The largest and most impressive of the units is the $1,099 Dyson HushJet Big+Quiet Cool Pure+Formaldehyde. The name is a mouthful, but it’s the company’s largest air purifier, with the most powerful compressor, designed to handle multiroom air purification and mixing. It even has wheels so it can be moved from room to room (it’s not self-propelled, unfortunately), and controls that let the nozzle-like head move and rotate in a way that’s vaguely reminiscent of a Dune sandworm. The head can tilt up and down, letting you angle the airflow for direct cooling or broader room circulation.

Dyson

Impressively, despite the unit’s sheer size, I didn’t really hear the airflow except at the highest settings. Meanwhile, the sheer amount of air it emitted through the large, open demo area was impressive. I could really feel the air circulating and starting to clear up without it feeling like I was being blown directly by a fan. The unit can capture 99.99% of pollutants down to 0.01 microns and destroy formaldehyde, a chemical byproduct that can be present in many homes. 

The medium-sized $599 HushJet Pure Cool+Formaldehyde is the unit I expect most people to get because it’s on the more reasonable side while still delivering powerful purification and cooling. Dyson says it can deliver three times the purification of predecessors and still clean large spaces while acting as a fan to provide personal cooling. 

The $599 HushJet Hot Cool Pure+ is similar, but it adds heating capabilities in addition to the purification and cooling. Dyson describes it as a three-in-one unit that can also be useful as a space heater in the winter, not just a fan in the summer.

All three Dyson HushJet models are expected to launch in fall 2026, and we look forward to testing them at CNET Labs.

Editors’ note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

fullText:
Apple has three new flagship iPhones launching next week: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and iPhone Ultra. Apple’s Pro models will have several advantages over the Ultra, but here are three ways the high-end Ultra will come out on top.

#1: Larger (and smaller) displays

Dummy models for iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max

iPhone Ultra will have two displays with the following rumored dimensions:

5.5-inch cover display

7.8-inch inner display

This compares to iPhone 18 Pro’s 6.3-inch screen and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max.

Essentially, iPhone Ultra provides both a larger display than the Pro models and also a smaller one. As a result, it will be the better choice for anyone wanting the largest iPhone screen. But it could also be a winner for fans of small phones, like the discontinued iPhone mini.

#2: Fits in any pocket, comfortable in-hand

iPhone 18 Pro, and especially iPhone 18 Pro Max, will be hit-or-miss in fitting pockets. This was already an issue with iPhone 17 Pro models. And while dimensions will largely be the same this year, rumors indicate the plateau could get even thicker to make room for the new camera system.

iPhone Ultra, meanwhile, will have a compact form factor when folded. It should fit in far more pockets with ease.

Additionally, the sleek, Air-inspired design of iPhone Ultra should be more comfortable in the hand than Apple’s bulkier Pro models.

#3: Exclusive multitasking features in iOS 27

iPad mini pictured

Though iPhone Ultra will have a few hardware drawbacks compared to iPhone 18 Pro, it’s likely in the software experience that it will earn its ‘Ultra’ branding.

Side-by-side apps are rumored to be an exclusive multitasking feature of iPhone Ultra. When unfolded, you’ll be able to keep two apps active on-screen at all times. Drag and drop will even be supported between apps.

iOS 27 also brings landscape support to lots of system apps for the first time, no doubt intended for iPhone Ultra though available on other models too. This will enable an iPad-like app experience on iPhone Ultra’s large 7.8-inch screen.

fullText:
Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m watching every minute of M. Night Shyamalan’s new YouTube video on the making of Signs, trying to convince myself I don’t need the Sonos Ace Ultra headphones, and using this helpful guide to finally install a local AI model on my M4 Pro Mac Mini.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Another Android Drop is here, and it comes with some legitimately useful new features. But one feels designed specifically for me and my forgetfulness, and I can’t wait to use it all the time.

	

Gemini has been updated to work with Find Hub, Google’s tool for tracking phones and other gadgets in the ecosystem, to remember the location of physical objects. “Hey Google, remember that I left my spare key inside the hollowed-out copy of Infinite Jest on my bookshelf.” I’m a big fan of these kinds of small, tangible improvements to Android that most people, not just those on the latest version or running a Pixel, will benefit from.

The other new features include a Motion Assist accessibility feature to counteract motion sickness in the car; a Gemini-powered Live Guide accessibility feature that uses AI to “offer descriptions of what’s in front of you”; and a Keep integration inside Google Messages that lets people co-create shopping or packing lists.

Read more: Pixel 11 series getting early September update, not Android 17 QPR1

✉️ Inbox

IFA is here, and that means there are a bunch of gadgets to talk about.

Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra launch with 185Hz panels, 8 Elite Gen 5 chips, and huge batteries. Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, used to be known for its lower-priced devices, but now that everything’s expensive, the company is leaning into specs. These feature massive batteries and, on the Ultra, an honest-to-goodness subwoofer that sounds pretty great.

Roku launches its first OLED TVs, available now starting at $999. Roku may be an advertising company at heart, but it still has to make hardware, and its latest TVs are OLEDs that are pretty competitive, and a lot cheaper. They’re also Amazon exclusives for now.

Sony’s new ULT Tower party speakers start at $450. I need to meet the person spending $1500 on a party speaker — because I want to attend that party.

Razer Prio is an Android and iPhone game controller that folds down to roughly the size of a credit card. I have a million portable game controllers, from multiple generations of the Razer Kishi to the Backbone One to basically anything 8BitDo releases. And yet I will still buy this because it looks so darn cute folded up.

Samsung’s latest Galaxy Book 6 starts at $799 with 8GB of RAM. The Korean giant, along with Dell, is announcing a MacBook Neo competitor powered by Intel’s ultra-efficient Wildcat Lake chips.

Govee’s new ceiling light and LED strips are mood boosters with some AI sprinkled in. Govee’s new ceiling light contains “vitality spectrum technology” to keep people more alert during the dark winter months. Will it work? You can pay $399 to find out.

Belkin says its new ‘BoostSolid’ Qi2 batteries last 3x longer than other magnetic power banks. The accessory company is leaning on solid-state battery tech to outlast the competition, which means less e-waste.

Belkin just released four Android Find Hub trackers; one is a full wallet

Philips Hue adds HDMI-free and 4K Sync Box, Nanoleaf partnership, and exciting app upgrades. I’m a big fan of Hue products, so these cheaper options are music to my ears.

Now, onto the news of the day.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so popular that Samsung is stealing parts from next year’s phones just to make more. A headline that feels perfectly tailored for 2026: Samsung’s unlikely ascension meets a component crisis that’s only getting worse.

Oppo Find X10 reportedly has an 8,000 mAh battery and top-tier specs for a ‘base’ flagship. Oppo has absolutely no chill, and I love it. Can’t wait for this one.

Gemini 3.8 Flash rolling out three weeks after last release. Google is fast-running its Gemini 3.x Flash releases in an effort to make us forget that its newest Pro model is nearly three months late.

MrBeast will try to survive ‘the planet’s most unforgiving landscapes’ using Gemini and Fitbit Air in deal with Google. Google should stick to partnering with the better Jimmy, in my opinion.

Pixel 11 series can now join the Android 17 QPR2 Beta. If you’re a Pixel 11 owner, you can now skip ahead to December’s upcoming Android release and join the blur club.

Google rolling out Pixel Watch 5 September update

Android Auto tests Quick Settings and hilarious ‘Jimothy’ weather Easter egg [Gallery]. Jimothy is a national hero, and I’m so glad he’s getting the respect he deserves.

Android Auto 17.6 update rolling out with redesigned logo [Gallery]

YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required. My phone’s most-used app is quickly becoming my TV’s most-used endpoint, and this is going to make it even easier to cast to it.

Google will not have to sell AdX business, but it will have to make changes. Despite Google being found guilty of running an illegal advertising monopoly, a judge is not forcing it to break up its ad business.

Google Home update restores support for older Chromecast streamers, Home Mini. 

WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking. Not a huge security issue, but one worth knowing if only to learn what setting to disable to prevent it from happening.

MapQuest is back, at the top of the charts, and rushing to add Android Auto support. Thought it was a one-night stand? Nope, MapQuest is in it for the long haul.

Google’s next Pixel Fold reportedly adopting the same crease-less display as Apple. But more importantly, will the next Pixel Fold revert back to its original passport shape? 

Google Pixel adding ‘Battery usage summaries,’ rolling out on Pixel 10 and newer

🇩🇪 Upcoming

It’s IFA time, which means the tech press and analysts convene in Berlin for bratwurst, bier, and briefings.

While 9to5Google covers a lot of the miscellany, we don’t typically get to the crazier stuff, like this Acer gaming handheld/netbook concept that will almost certainly never be made.

TP-Link unveiled the first production Wi-Fi 8 routers far before most people have upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 (and given the speed of the rollout may skip it altogether). And Homey, the Dutch smart home accessory vendor recently acquired by LG, announced a controller hub that looks almost exactly like a Nest thermostat but does a whole lot more.

You can check out all of 9to5Google’s IFA 2026 coverage throughout the rest of the week.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

If you told me that the leaked DLSS 5 Neural Rendering tool would be ported to the Switch, I probably would have absolutely believed you because the internet is full of weird, smart people who just want to try things. Take a look at a yassified Mario from Mario Kart World or Link from Tears of the Kingdom looking sharper than ever.

I have rarely taken xAI’s Grok models seriously because from my understanding they were primarily used by Reply Guys to ask @grok what movie was being vagueposted. But in recent months, the company’s ties with and recent acquisition of Cursor have given Grok 4.6 serious coding and productivity chops. title: Apple pundits say Vision Pro is by far the best way to watch baseball
snippet: Both Apple pundits and most of the internet seem to agree that Vision Pro is the best way to watch baseball, following the immersive experience offered by Apple’s Friday Night Baseball. Notably, there also seemed to be a consensus view that less is more when it comes to the various immersive camera angles … more…
fullText:
Both Apple pundits and most of the internet seem to agree that Vision Pro is the best way to watch baseball, following the immersive experience offered by Apple’s Friday Night Baseball.

Notably, there also seemed to be a consensus view that less is more when it comes to the various immersive camera angles …

Macworld’s Michael Simon got the headline award with Apple finally hits the VR home run.

I’ve never had a desire to buy a Vision Pro. Even if I had $4,000 to blow at the Apple Store, I’d probably pick up a loaded MacBook Pro or a Mac mini with a Studio Display XDR instead of Apple’s cutting-edge handset. But Friday Night Baseball in Apple Immersive changed my perspective. The first-ever broadcast of a live Major League Baseball game with 3D video recorded in 8K with a 180-degree field of view, watching the Red Sox-Yankees game on the Vision Pro was almost as breathtaking as being at Yankee Stadium.

Daring Fireball’s John Gruber was every bit as enthusiastic.

The whole thing was legit exciting. Vision Pro continues to get a bad rap because Apple hasn’t sold many of them, and isn’t going to sell many of them until they come out with new models that are cheaper and lighter and less fussy. But there’s no denying that these immersive experiences are fucking cool. And an immersive live experience adds something else. It’s ineffable. Hard to say why, but feeling like you’re at another place watching something happen live is magic. Just a few years ago it would have required literal magic. It wasn’t possible. Now it is.

Jason Snell at Six Colors was more restrained in his phrasing, but was also a fan.

In the end, it felt much more like I was sitting at Yankee Stadium watching the game. 

He said one change Apple made over its basketball footage was not cutting between lots of different camera angles, and he fully approved. Others agreed with him.

Each half inning was shown from a single camera on the dugout rail next to the on-deck circle, giving a great view of pitcher and hitter and the infield, as well as the goings on right in front of the dugout in foul territory. The camera switched between innings, so you were always viewing from the perspective of the at-bat team’s dugout. Making it all work better was Apple’s addition of a “virtual jumbotron” floating in the sky, a scoreboard with graphics and a video feed of the standard 16:9 telecast on Apple TV. It was easy to look up and catch a replay or even get a better view of something happening in the far-off outfield, without getting in the way of my view of the game itself.

Having watched a clip posted on X by Justin Ryan of Spatial Insider, this does seem to offer the best of both worlds.

Live immersive MLB on Apple Vision Pro. It felt like I was at Yankee Stadium. The whole experience was incredible.

Shot through the lens with iPhone since it can’t be recorded on headset. pic.twitter.com/oF1J9tBTd8

— Justin Ryan (@justinryanio) August 29, 2026

As someone who thinks a far less expensive and massively lighter face monitor is a better bet for most TV and movie viewing, I can definitely see the appeal of Vision Pro for this type of fully immersive experience. I’m still waiting for my perfect compromise product.

title: AAPL gained 2,736% under Cook, but Ternus doesn’t have to emulate him
snippet: Bloomberg carries a piece noting the astonishing gains made by Apple stockholders during the time when Tim Cook was CEO. The cumulative gain was 2,275% – or a total return of 2,736% when accounting for dividend payments also. The site suggests this will make him a tough act to follow, but my own view is that new CEO John Ternus doesn’t have to emulate Cook’s management of the company … more…
fullText:
Bloomberg carries a piece noting the astonishing gains made by Apple stockholders during the time when Tim Cook was CEO. The cumulative gain was 2,275% – or a total return of 2,736% when accounting for dividend payments also.

The site suggests this will make him a tough act to follow, but my own view is that new CEO John Ternus doesn’t have to emulate Cook’s management of the company … 

There’s no disputing the numbers Bloomberg cites.

Cook inherited a company with a market capitalization of less than $350 billion and built the maker of iPhones and Mac computers into a diverse $4.6 trillion business that also sells watches, AirPods and financial services […] During his time as CEO, the shares climbed a whopping 2,736% on a total-return basis.

But my stance is that John Ternus shouldn’t for one moment worry about whether Apple will emulate this degree of financial success under his leadership – and there are two reasons for this.

First, both of his key predecessors argued that financial success is a side effect of the true goal, not something that should be chased directly. Steve Jobs famously said:

“If you focus on making really great products, then the profits will follow.”

Cook himself has echoed this philosophy, saying that he never worried about quarterly results, but instead focused on the long-term direction of the company.

Second, the advice Steve gave to Tim when he took over:

“Don’t ask what I would do. Just do the right thing.”

Ternus shouldn’t ask himself what either Jobs or Cook would have done. He should instead  run Apple in the way that he thinks is most likely to see the successful development of the best possible products, and the evolution of the best company culture and values for long-term success. 

I suspect he will be a very different CEO to Cook, just as Cook was to Jobs. The goal isn’t to try to emulate past formulae, but instead to look ahead and – to borrow a phrase from the outgoing CEO – follow his own North Star.

Do you share my view or have a different perspective? Please let us know your thoughts in the comments.

title: Apple Maps now uses ‘Lake America’ instead of ‘Lake Ontario’ after Trump order
snippet: If you head to Apple Maps today, you’ll notice that Apple has started renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The move follows Trump’s order last week to change the name as part of an ongoing trade dispute with Canada. more…
fullText:
If you head to Apple Maps today, you’ll notice that Apple has started renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” The move follows Trump’s order last week to change the name as part of an ongoing trade dispute with Canada.

The change, which was first spotted by Bloomberg, applies for Apple Maps users in the United States. Apple Maps users in Canada will still see the “Lake Ontario” name. Apple Maps users elsewhere around the world will see both names.  

Google Maps changed Lake Ontario to Lake America several days ago. At the time, Google said that its policy is to use the names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said yesterday that Trump had “reached out to Apple directly” about making this change. That conversation seems to have led Apple to follow suit and change the name in Apple Maps as well.

MapQuest, meanwhile, said this week that it refuses to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, which has led to a surge in downloads.

The change appears to be rolling out to Apple Maps users gradually. On my iPhone, I still see Lake Ontario, while others on the 9to5Mac team already see Lake America.

When Trump ordered the renaming of the Gulf of Mexico to “Gulf of America” last year, Apple also followed suit on Apple Maps.

title: TikTok comments are getting more interactive with voice comments, polls, and more
snippet: With the additions, the app is borrowing features from messaging apps as it looks to deepen engagement on its platform.
fullText:
TikTok’s comment sections are getting an upgrade. The social network announced on Thursday that it’s rolling out new features for its comment sections, including voice comments, comment polls, photo carousel comments, and Live Photo comments.

With the additions, the app is borrowing features from messaging apps as it looks to deepen engagement on its platform. By bundling voice, polls, and photo comments, the company aims to make comment sections places where people linger and interact with each other, rather than simply leave feedback underneath a video.

“Sound and music have shaped TikTok from the very beginning, turning songs into trends and audio clips into jokes shared across the app,” TikTok wrote in a blog post. “Now, we’re bringing that same energy to the comment section with Voice Comments, a new way to post and listen to audio messages directly under any video.”

Image Credits:TikTok

To leave a voice comment, users need to tap the microphone icon in the comment box and record a message up to a minute long. Once the voice comment is posted, anyone can tap to listen.

A TikTok spokesperson told TechCrunch that voice comments are subject to the same Community Guidelines as other content on the platform. The company uses a combination of human and automated detection tools, including speech-to-text transcription, to identify and remove content that violates its policies.

Voice comments are rolling out globally over the next month to users 18 and older. 

Additionally, creators can now add a poll when commenting on their own videos, a feature that had been previously available to some, but is now available globally. 

TikTok says the polls can be used for things like voting on the next video idea, picking an outfit, deciding what to cook, and more. Creators can choose up to five options for viewers to vote on and then set a time frame for the poll. As votes come in, creators can follow results directly in the comment section.

Image Credits:TikTok

With photo carousel comments, people can now add up to nine photos in a single comment, after previously only being able to add one at a time. Plus, users can now upload Live Photo comments, which TikTok says will allow for “a brief burst of motion” that allows others to see a quick preview of the moment before viewing the full image.

Live Photo comments are now available globally, while photo carousel comments are rolling out globally over the next month.

That's fast enough to record 4K Apple ProRes video at up to 120fps when conn … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Following the lead of companies like Xteink, Lexar is the latest to sacrifice a USB-C port in the pursuit of slimming down its hardware.

When the Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD launches later this year in 512GB and 1TB capacities it will be one of the slimmest you can buy. At its thickest point in the middle it measures just 3.8mm, but that tapers to only 1mm at the edges thanks to high-density NAND stacking and a “custom ultra-thin PCB architecture” inside. But performance remains solid with read speeds up to 1,050MB/s and write speeds maxing out at 1,000MB/s. That’s fast enough to record 4K Apple ProRes video at up to 120fps when connected to a compatible iPhone.

The downside is that without a standard USB-C port, you’ll need to rely on — and make sure not to lose — Lexar’s proprietary SnapLink cable that magnetically attaches to a pogo-pin connector on the side of the drive. The company doesn’t specify the strength of the magnets, but this approach also means there’s an increased risk of the cable being accidentally knocked off during a file transfer. And if you are using the Muse to record videos through your phone, you’ll need to slip it into an included magnetic sleeve in order to mount it to the back of your device, adding quite a bit of thickness in the process.

title: MapQuest is back, at the top of the charts, and rushing to add Android Auto support
snippet: In a “that’s a name I’ve not heard in a long time” move, MapQuest is back to being a household name, as the original mapping app has found itself as the top of app store charts – it’s also rushing to add support for Android Auto. more…
fullText:
In a “that’s a name I’ve not heard in a long time” move, MapQuest is back to being a household name, as the original mapping app has found itself as the top of app store charts – it’s also rushing to add support for Android Auto.

MapQuest has been around for 30 years, but it only entered the modern era back in 2024 when it relaunched with a private mobile mapping app with a pitch around being “anti-Big Tech.” That app has since shut down, and a full MapQuest app arrived earlier this year.

Now, that app is at the top of app store charts.

On iOS, MapQuest is the #8 free app on the App Store (as of Aug 30), and #5 on Android’s Play Store (as of today) – at least in the US. In a press release, MapQuest says this is “the highest chart position in the brand’s 30-year history” and that usage is “roughly 50 times its normal rate.” 

	

Why the sudden surge? Even MapQuest acknowledges it’s mostly to do with a rejection of “Lake America,” with the brand refusing to update “Lake Ontario” on its platform in the wake of a recent executive order in the US which Google Maps and more recently Apple Maps have updated their maps to show. The viral nature of that stand reminded many that MapQuest even still exists, and brought about this wave of popularity.

In a bid to keep users on its app, MapQuest confirmed that it is rapidly building out support for Android Auto – it already supports CarPlay on iPhone. Android Auto added support for third-party navigation apps a few years ago, and there are quite a few options available.

MapQuest still lags behind Google Maps and others in terms of live transit and other features, but supports turn-by-turn navigation, live traffic data, and more. MapQuest is currently owned by System1, an advertising company.

Apple’s Calendar app has stayed remarkably consistent over the years. The app tends to get new features less often than other popular Apple apps. And its design has changed very little over the years, even looking largely the same after last year’s Liquid Glass update.

But in iOS 27, Apple has notable design changes coming in two main areas:

Event details view

Event creation and editing

As seen in the image above, when you tap on any calendar event, the details view has gotten a revamp.

Information has been reorganized in a way that lets you view more details on-screen at a time. The addition of icons is a helpful visual cue that makes everything easier to parse. These changes, combined with smaller design updates, add up to a more modern overall feel.

iOS 27 also brings similar design updates when creating or editing events in Calendar.

As the image on the left shows, more information now fits on-screen and it’s all been reorganized and refreshed.

Icons are put to good use here, just like in the event details view. And you’ll notice headings now organize event parameters in a way that makes everything easier to navigate.

Beyond these two areas, the Calendar app also benefits from iOS 27’s systemwide enhancements to Liquid Glass. Overall, the update brings some of Calendar’s most noteworthy design changes in years.

title: Upgrade paths: Should Pixel 9 owners upgrade to Pixel 11? [Video]
snippet: We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here. Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video] more…
fullText:
We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here.

Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video]

Your 24-month cell plan might be coming to an end, so it’s timely to talk about this switch now, and we’ll do our best to help you decide which phone is right, which phone is wrong, and ultimately whether an upgrade is worthwhile.

An unchanged design

Let’s get the obvious out of the way at the start: the Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro are very, very similar. You could be forgiven for thinking they are the same. For anyone with a non-Pro phone, you’ll see more pronounced changes, but for all intents and purposes, the designs are almost identical across the entire device lineup.

Let’s get into the actual improvements. No matter what Pixel 9 phone you have, all Pixel 11 displays are better. Maybe not drastically so, but you get a jump up in maximum brightness of around 10% on the Pixel 9 to 11. The Pros get a 20% brightness jump at peak. This is something you probably would notice, but still not a major change. All the screens are well tuned, there’s no bezel reduction, just the same great experience, but brighter.

	

We know the design is the same, the core frame dimensions are identical, the same height, width, and thickness. The only visible change is in the camera bar shape and size. You can’t use your old cases on the new phone, so that is an annoyance. The Pixel 9 and 11 are within 1g, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL are almost 10 grams heavier than the 9 Pro and Pro XL. 

That could be due to the marginal battery size increases and maybe even the addition of Pixelsnap magnets, but it’s likely some internal changes that add a little extra mass, and better thermals too. Pixelsnap is great for connectivity, but a good case can mimic it pretty closely on the Pixel 9.

Similar software experience

One of the key differences between the Pixel 9 and Pixel 11 is Gemini Intelligence. It’s emblazoned all over the latest phone and adds some functionality that likely won’t come to the older devices unless Google has a change of heart.

You need to figure out if you care enough about some of the AI tools like App Automation, Rambler, the enhanced Proactive Assistant responses and replies for messaging, plus some of the other enhancements that the Pixel 10 added last year.

Some of this is merely fluff. Some are great features. Do they drastically improve your life? That remains to be seen.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 11: Where are the upgrades? [Video]

Even the move from Tensor G4 up to the G6 chip might not be a big enough leap for lots of people. Neither is an amazing performance beast, but they’re competent chips that handle most things you’ll throw at either phone.

Faster storage is arguably a bigger ingredient in the equation because apps will load faster, and you also get the benefit of a 256GB base model now. It was a long-overdue quality of life change that will make a bigger difference in the long term.

Frustratingly, getting less RAM on the Pixel 11 Pro or Pro XL versus the Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL feels like a slap in the face. It’s not necessarily noticeable right now, save that you can have more apps in memory. Some of the RAM is wired for AI task control, so you’ll lose out here unless you pay more to get 16GB RAM.

The fact is, though, that the performance gap is not exactly a chasm, and Android 17 is identical here. Unless Google specifies otherwise, you’ll get all the same updates in the future too.

Quality cameras continue to impress

If you want a telephoto lens and have the Pixel 9, then yes, you might want to upgrade. The digital zoom is not as good on the base 9. It’s capped and isn’t going to get close to the action.

The other lenses are fairly similar, but know that the main sensor is slightly larger on the Pixel 11. With the default settings, it’s a toss-up.

Camera Looks are where we get some notable improvements. These are sensor-level filters that you can customize to tune your Pixel 11 camera output. No Pixel 9 will get these tools. It’s arguably the biggest change on a Pixel camera since the addition of a triple camera setup.

If you have a Pro phone, there is a better telephoto lens that lets you zoom up to 120X. Video modes get some upgrades, AI-powered Magic Capture, plus a new Creator Mode is here too.

Like basically every other head-to-head comparison, the camera improvements are more about refinement than redefining, which makes a Pixel camera so reliable.

I don’t think someone would be disappointed at what has changed, maybe underwhelmed given the two-year leap. The reality is that a Pixel camera has mostly been about consistency, which hasn’t changed.

Is now the time to upgrade from the Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

You don’t need us to tell you that the generational “leaps” are becoming less and less pronounced, even if you skip a few new releases.

Whether brands are holding certain functions back or other factors are at play is a topic rife among practically any industry observer right now. AI is playing a big role in the physical hardware you will buy now and for years to come.

In our eyes, there is only one key reason you should consider making the switch from a Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11, and that is if your phone is on its last legs or if you have the base 9 and want a telephoto lens. Those are the only two major reasons someone should consider the jump.

The Pixel 9 Pro and Pro XL are still fine phones. There seems to be no major or widespread issues that might cause people to be desperate to upgrade or switch away. It wasn’t the best phone on the market at launch, but, like any Pixel before, these devices tend to age better than others thanks to updates and enhancements courtesy of Google’s now-extensive support window.

If you’re even considering ditching a Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL for the Pixel 11 lineup, think hard about what you’re actually getting. There isn’t anything on the software front that really warrants the substantial price increase. The new modem is good, but not a quantum leap. The camera improvements don’t provide exponential gains for photography or videography.

This is also true of most other pieces of tech right now. If your cell plan or contract is coming to an end imminently, maybe a cheap SIM plan could be a way to save cash at a time when smartphones are ballooning in price thanks to the constant march of AI development and the costs associated with the expansion.

The truth is that a two-generation upgrade cycle makes little sense today. You will simply get more bang for your buck by hanging on for another year. A battery replacement or repair would likely provide more value in most cases, given how little has truly changed over the past couple of years.

title: Here’s how much Apple is paying John Ternus as CEO, Tim Cook as executive chairman
snippet: In a new regulatory filing today, Apple revealed that new CEO John Ternus is receiving a pay package with $58 million in salary and target stock awards. The company also shared details on Tim Cook’s lucrative new deal as Apple’s executive chairman. more…
fullText:
In a new regulatory filing today, Apple revealed that new CEO John Ternus is receiving a pay package with $58 million in salary and target stock awards. The company also shared details on Tim Cook’s lucrative new deal as Apple’s executive chairman.

John Ternus’s new compensation

The numbers were disclosed in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission today. Ternus’s $58 million pay package includes two components:

Base salary: $3 million/year

Annual equity award: $55 million target value beginning fiscal 2027

75% ($41.25M) performance-based restricted stock units (RSUs)

25% ($13.75M) time-based RSUs

The performance shares depend on Apple’s total shareholder return compared with other S&P 500 companies. The time-based shares vest 12.5% every six months over four years.

For 2026, Ternus is also receiving prorated stock awards with a $2.5 million target value, covering the portion of fiscal 2026 he serves as CEO.

While Apple did not disclose Ternus’s previous salary in his role as senior vice president of hardware engineering, Bloomberg reports “that management level typically gets paid about $25 million annually when including stock, salary and bonuses.”

Tim Cook’s new compensation

Meanwhile, Tim Cook is receiving a pay package with a $47 million target value for fiscal 2027. This includes:

Base salary: $2 million/year, effective September 26

Fiscal 2027 equity award: $45 million target value

50% ($22.5M) performance-based

50% ($22.5M) time-based, vesting 12.5% every six months over four years

This is an unusually large pay package for an executive chairman role, signaling the value that Apple thinks Cook brings to the table here. Cook’s focus as executive chairman will see him managing Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government.

For fiscal 2025, Cook’s total pay package as CEO was $74,294,811. That number, however, includes things not factored into today’s SEC filing. Those include non-equity incentive plan compensation, retirement plans, vacation days, personal security expenses, and more. Cook’s salary and stock awards totaled roughly $60.5 million for 2025.

title: Report: Apple Watch Series 12 may feature always-on heart-rate tracking, new Fitness app
snippet: According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has a couple new features in the pipeline for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 that’ll make it much more appealing for health-conscious users. The company is also testing two finishes for the rumored ceramic version. more…
fullText:
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has a couple new features in the pipeline for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 that’ll make it much more appealing for health-conscious users. The company is also testing two finishes for the rumored ceramic version.

New health upgrades

These two key health upgrades will likely sound appealing if you’re someone who’s dissatisfied with the state of Apple Watch as a fitness tracker. The two features are always-on heart-rate tracking, and an all new app design. that’ll make it much easier to learn from your health data. Here’s how Gurman describes the new app:

Apple is also working on revamping its fitness and health app software to show more wellness-related metrics in a similar fashion to increasingly popular app offerings from Whoop and Oura.

As someone who currently owns a WHOOP, I will say my primary draw to it has always been the fact that I find it much easier to learn from my health data in the WHOOP app. It’ll show me all of the factors that make my sleep or recovery poor, whereas with Apple Watch it feels the only important thing is your activity rings. If Apple makes meaningful progress in this regard, I’ll be quite happy.

A key part of making the Apple Watch a more data-rich experience is well, having more data. Apple is reportedly testing the ability for the heart-rate sensor to record all day, rather than only during workouts and at random.

Two new finishes

We’ve already heard that Apple is weighing ceramic for the Apple Watch Series 12, though Gurman is now reporting that there’ll be two color options: the traditional white, as well as a dark gray color. There’ll also be “many new band colors and configurations.”

Redesign in the future

The current Apple Watch design language was introduced in 2024, with the Apple Watch Series 12. It was a relatively modest shift, with the company making the watch much thinner at the compromise of bezels. According to Bloomberg, we may see a new Apple Watch redesign next year with the Series 13, though it could shift to the Series 14:

Apple is pushing to have a big redesign for its watch ready by next year, but things could still slip to the year after.

I am quite excited to see what Apple cooks up here. It does feel like they’ve about peaked at what they can do with the rounded off design language, so maybe we’ll see a new shape entirely. Hopefully it doesn’t break backwards compatibility with older watch bands.

title: Syncing Hue lights to your TV now starts at $120; Nanoleaf integration too
snippet: Syncing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display used to be a rather expensive undertaking, at $385 for the company’s Sync Box 8K. A couple of new products now bring that cost down to as little as $120. Additionally, you can now integrate Nanoleaf wall panels into your Philips Hue ecosystem thanks to a new $40 Wall Light Module … more…
fullText:
Syncing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display used to be a rather expensive undertaking, at $385 for the company’s Sync Box 8K. A couple of new products now bring that cost down to as little as $120.

Additionally, you can now integrate Nanoleaf wall panels into your Philips Hue ecosystem thanks to a new $40 Wall Light Module … 

Syncing Hue lights to your TV

Synchronizing your Philips Hue lights to your TV display can create an extremely immersive experience for anything from movies to games.

The company’s Sync Box 8K uses HDMI signals to detect the colors displayed on your TV screen and then adjusts all of the Hue lighting in the same room to match in real time. At almost $400, however, it’s an expensive option, and the bundles with Gradient Light Strips can reach over $650 for the largest TVs.

The company is now offering two more affordable options:

Sync Box 4K, which also uses an HDMI signal: $150

Play Screen Sync, which uses a camera: $120

HDMI syncing is the more accurate approach, and the new 4K model reduces costs by reducing support from four HDMI feeds to just one. The maximum supported resolution is 4K at 60Hz. 

The Play Screen Sync supports whatever is being displayed, but the color matching accuracy is compromised. There are already third-party products from companies like Govee using this approach.

Nanoleaf integration

The Verge spotted that a new Wall Light Module has been jointly launched by Philips and Nanoleaf. The $40 box makes any Nanoleaf product appear to be a Philips Hue device.

While Nanoleaf products already have HomeKit support, adding Hue compatibility can be useful for third-party apps which offer more flexibility with things like animated scenes and music syncing.

title: XREAL has set the perfect stage for Android XR
snippet: I’ve always been a bit skeptical of smart glasses and mixed reality headsets. It’s not hard to find the utility of something like a Meta Quest in gaming, but Apple’s Vision Pro, for example, has never appealed to me in the slightest. Ahead of its first pair of Android XR glasses, though, I’ve spent some time with the XREAL One Pro and two things have become immediately clear – this is the hardware that could make Android XR shine, and XREAL will benefit greatly from Android XR. more…
fullText:
I’ve always been a bit skeptical of smart glasses and mixed reality headsets. It’s not hard to find the utility of something like a Meta Quest in gaming, but Apple’s Vision Pro, for example, has never appealed to me in the slightest. Ahead of its first pair of Android XR glasses, though, I’ve spent some time with the XREAL One Pro and two things have become immediately clear – this is the hardware that could make Android XR shine, and XREAL will benefit greatly from Android XR.

If you’re unfamiliar with XREAL, I actually can’t blame you one bit. I always knew about this company, but the idea of glasses that put a screen in front of my face never sounded particularly worthwhile to me. But when XREAL mentioned it would adopt Android XR, I just had to give this tech a shot.

So, lately, I’ve been using XREAL One Pro, plugged into either a Galaxy Z Fold 7, MacBook, or a Redmagic Astra 2 tablet. The idea is really that simple. Whatever you’re doing, just plug it into the glasses and see it pop up on a 157-inch display (customizable) in front of your face. Initially, I wasn’t all that sure I’d find it useful, but a clear use case did immediately come up – airplanes.

Having a giant screen that floats in front of you and follows your movements is just so perfect in that context. It sure beats a seatback screen, and wearing them for a few hours on a flight is pretty comfortable too.

	

I’d never do this with a full headset, it’s just too bulky and weird-looking. XREAL One Pro don’t exactly look “normal.” They stick out from your face a little too far to be subtle, but the compact size in your bag and the cable running down makes it pretty clear what’s going on. 

These still don’t look normal, but they’re way less goofy than a VR headset
This is so much easier to transport compared to a VR headset

As for the actual quality, it’s pretty great. Like any screen in front of your face, it takes a minute to dial in the settings, but movies look great once you do. Mirroring my MacBook screen also made a great full-size canvas to do some work, all without worrying about the person in front of me reclining and ruining the whole experience. It’s not perfect, as while XREAL’s 3DoF tracking is fantastic on the ground, it has a tendency to drift around while on a flight, especially if there’s any turbulence.

The only trouble comes from the unfortunate fact that not everything works. When plugged into the Redmagic tablet, for instance, I ran into problems with certain video apps including Fandango at Home and Google TV, though the latter worked fine on my Fold over DeX. The 3D conversion mode also never worked on the Redmagic tablet, though it was pretty solid when it did work on my Fold.

You can change how much of the real world you see, no cameras needed

And I think that’s where XREAL Aura with Android XR will “complete” the experience.

XREAL One Pro just builds on whatever you feed into it. The on-board controls and software are limited, and you simply can’t do anything without your secondary device. There are add-ons for gesture controls, and XREAL sells an Android phone that adds a UI to the glasses, but I think Android XR truly is the missing puzzle piece. XREAL seems to agree, as the company is pretty vocal about its vision for the future involving a lot more Android XR. And it’s not like the ability to plug in a device will go away, as Aura is set to support that.

There’s absolutely still space for what we have today. As mentioned, the simple ability to watch movies or get a bigger laptop display on the go rocks. But that’s where something like XREAL’s new A01+ glasses can shine, and for a lot less money at $299. I wouldn’t fork over $600 for XREAL One Pro just to get a bigger screen I can throw in my bag, but I’d definitely pay for the A01+, and XREAL 1S at $450 is also worth considering – I tried those out back at CES, and they work just about as well as One Pro, at least for the purposes I’ve mentioned here.

XREAL Aura is set to launch later this year, while One Pro, 1S, and A01+, are all available now.

Have you tried these out? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

title: Gemini Notebook switching to compute-based usage limits, like Gemini app
snippet: Following the Gemini app in May, Gemini Notebook is switching to “compute-specific usage limits” starting in September. more…
fullText:
Following the Gemini app in May, Gemini Notebook is switching to “compute-specific usage limits” starting in September.

Related: Google announces ‘Expert Intelligence’ to let you add Play Books in Gemini Notebook

This system replaces the set number of feature generations per day that depended on your Google AI tier. Limits refresh every five hours “rather than daily.” 

Google explains that “your overall usage limit will factor in prompt complexity, chat length, number of sources, and the features you use.” Notebooks will “help you keep track of your usage,” with a status appearing below the chat: 

“You’re almost at your AI usage limit. Limit resets at 3:00 PM.”

“Limit reached. All features are available after 3:00 PM.”

Another indicator will appear at the bottom of Studio generations to show expected AI usage cost: “The more the bar is filled in, the higher the expected cost.”

	

Gemini Notebook will “suggest alternative outputs if your first choice surpasses your limit.” There’s also “Generate later” to “defer generating outputs,” like intensive Video Overviews or Slide Decks. Google will automatically create them once your limit resets, with this feature coming first to the web. 

Free/Without a plan: Standard limits

Google AI Plus: 2x higher than standard limits

Google AI Pro: 4x higher than standard limits

Google AI Ultra: 5x or 20x higher than AI Pro depending on your subscription

The new compute-based usage limits will start rolling out to consumer accounts on web and mobile on September 2.

title: Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video]
snippet: More of the same isn’t always a bad thing, but in some cases it could be. Does that ring true with the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro? Find out here. more…
fullText:
More of the same isn’t always a bad thing, but in some cases it could be. Does that ring true with the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro? Find out here.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 10 Pro: Closer together than ever? [Video]

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Hardware

We’re looking at some very similar designs again for 2026 and 2027. Yes, the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro look like the Pixel 10, which in turn looked like the Pixel 9. That’s not to say some changes haven’t been made, the most important is to the camera bar.

The outer frame is metal, but the “bar” is glass. Google also slimmed down the thickness of the Pixel 11 camera bar. It’s thinner and doesn’t stick out quite as much. The Pixel 11 Pro camera bar still protrudes. This is something to consider, as although supported cases work on both phones, the Pixel 11 Pro camera sticks out more and could be in harm’s way. You should check that any third-party case is fully compatible with both models before picking one up.

	

The Pixel 11 Pro has a higher-resolution 1280 x 2856 panel, while the base Pixel 11 stays at 1080 x 2424. The cheaper phone has thicker bezels, and because it’s not LTPO — supporting a 60–120Hz refresh rate instead — it lacks some of the hyper-dynamic refresh rate changes that the Pro’s 1–120Hz LTPO display offers. 

They are both super bright panels, though, reaching up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness on the base Pixel 11 and an illuminating 3,600 nits on the Pixel 11 Pro. For protection, the base model still uses standard Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2, but the Pro adds a specialized anti-scratch coating on top of its Victus 2 glass, delivering more than double the scratch resistance compared to previous models. Even so, a screen protector might still feel necessary in our experience if you’re going to use the HiLight feature, which requires your phone to be face down.

There are a few things to be aware of spec-wise. The base Pixel 11 comes standard with 12GB of RAM and storage options of 256GB or 512GB. The Pixel 11 Pro runs similarly at the entry-level, shipping with 12GB of RAM for its 256GB storage option. 

That is down from 16GB on the Pixel 10 Pro, and if you want Google’s top-tier performance configuration, only the 512 GB and 1 TB models of the Pro step up to 16 GB of RAM. One bonus is that all models now have UFS 4.0 storage by default on the entry-level tier of either phone. Google has locked even faster storage performance to higher tiers, meaning you must upgrade to at least the 512 GB tier on either model to get the benefit of Zoned UFS.

Other little things to be aware of are that the Pixel 11 has Wi-Fi 6E connectivity, while the Pixel 11 Pro has Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, and it also has UWB support for better Bluetooth connectivity and some benefits when using digital car keys.

The Pixel 11 Pro also has HiLight. To be frank, this is just a colorful LED integrated into the flash. It serves as an indicator for Gemini and calls when face down in Flip to Shh mode. A basic, limited notification LED. That’s all it does at launch.

Software

There is zero change between how the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro look and feel. Android 17 is identical, even down to all of the core features and functions. The Pro doesn’t get anything extra. There may be some benefits with the addition of Zoned UFS with the 512GB and 1TB models, or long-term performance gains if you pick the 16GB RAM version.

HiLight gives you some extra controls for the color tuning of the rear notification LED. This is limited, but it works only in the Contacts application as of today. Further compatibility is expected in the coming months.

There’s the default promise of seven years of OS, security, and Pixel Drop updates. So, at least in theory, expect these phones to get OTAs until August 2033. Whether the hardware will last that long is another question entirely.

Brand-new AI features introduced on the Pixel 11 series include Gemini Intelligence for proactive task offloading, allowing you to delegate routine tasks like restaurant reservations or compare shared apartment and hotel links directly inside your text chats. 

Gboard’s Rambler voice-to-text tool cleans up spoken filler words, alongside Gboard’s Sign-to-Text input, which translates sign language in real time using the front-facing Pixel Camera.

For photo and video creation, both models benefit from the new conversational, Gemini-powered Edit with Ask Photos, sensor-level film aesthetics with fully customizable Camera Looks, and the comprehensive video production tools of the Creator Suite.

Lastly, they both feature the brand-new Magic Capture mode to automatically extract the five best HDR+ frames from a short video clip and real-time 4K Portrait bokeh video, ensuring you don’t miss out on these cutting-edge flagship innovations by choosing the base model

Battery

A couple of things stand out right away with the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro. Firstly, the base model has a bigger battery at 4,985 mAh compared to the Pixel 11 Pro’s 4,850 mAh. We don’t even know the reason for this change because they retain identical physical footprints (both measuring 6.0 x 2.8 x 0.3 inches).

Both support fast charging up to 55% in about 30 minutes with a 30W USB-C PPS charger or higher, which, let’s be honest, is still somewhat slow by modern Android smartphone standards.

The upgraded Qi2.2-certified Pixelsnap wireless charging means you now get up to the full 25W rate on both models. This delivers up to 25% faster wireless charging on the base Pixel 11 and up to 29% faster on the Pixel 11 Pro compared to their predecessors. That doesn’t seem like much, but is great for Pixelsnap charger owners.

Camera

For a lot of people, the camera is where you’ll likely decide which Pixel 11 or 11 Pro phone is going to be what you want or need. The Pixel 11 has a new 48MP main sensor, but retains the same 13MP ultrawide and 10.8MP 5x telephoto from the Pixel 10. The new main is a big jump back up from the disappointing 10MP main from the base model a year prior. It offers 56% increase in light sensitivity, so it is just a better sensor all around.

The telephoto hasn’t changed, but Super Zoom is now supported up to 30x on the base Pixel 11, which is a nice bump up from the 20x limit on the previous generation. Google says this is thanks to the Tensor G6 chip.

While software tuning and the improved primary sensor help the phone, you will still get a vastly superior camera experience on the Pixel 11 Pro over the standard Pixel 11, no matter how you cut it.

On the Pixel 11 Pro, Google has packed a much more advanced triple array, including a redesigned 48 MP telephoto camera that pulls in 32% more light. This improved lens enables up to 120x Pro Zoom, combining Tensor G6 hardware with the latest AI imaging models to improve blocky, long-distance photos with a level of clarity that is impressive if a little artificial. 

Fortunately, you don’t lose out on some of Google’s best shooting guidance on the cheaper option, as Camera Looks are still here, Magic Camera, Portrait Blur video, and the Creator Mode are available. It misses out on the Instant Night Sight, Video Boost, Super Res Zoom Video, 

If you want the best Pixel photos and videos, the choice remains simple: the Pixel 11 Pro is far more capable than the standard Pixel 11.

Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: Which should I choose?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

It’s a tough year to be a smartphone buyer. There are some difficult decisions you will have to make where an upgrade is concerned, and the Pixel 11 lineup signifies this much more than almost any other recent release.

The Pixel 11 doesn’t feel like it has been held back this year like the Pixel 10 was. You get enough functionality to get within touching distance of the Pixel 11 Pro. Most people will be really well-suited to the base model, because it has some important upgrades.

Being able to stomach the price jumps is another problem entirely. The Pixel 11 Pro is now well over $1,000. The Pixel 11 starts at an eye-watering $899 in the US, which is very high for what you get. There is a lot of settling within either price bracket this time.

Last year’s phones might provide you with substantially more bang for your buck because you’re still getting 90% of the Pixel 11 at under 70% of the cost. If you must have Google’s latest phones, wait a little while until we see sales and further discounts. Some trade-in deals have softened the blow of the RAM downgrades and price increases, so be sure to shop around for a deal that works for you – or check out the best current deals below.
