title: Review: The Pixel 11 Pro XL is great, but a little too early for Google’s futuristic vision
snippet: At this point, phones have been boring for long enough that even calling them boring feels a little passé. The days of smartphones feeling like the cutting edge of technology are long gone, replaced with iterative updates and a big focus on software-as-a-service. Disconnecting from your smartphone might not seem too difficult on its face, but from rideshare apps to mobile payments, today’s solutions tend to leave a lot more gaps in your life than you might otherwise expect. more…
fullText:
At this point, phones have been boring for long enough that even calling them boring feels a little passé. The days of smartphones feeling like the cutting edge of technology are long gone, replaced with iterative updates and a big focus on software-as-a-service. Disconnecting from your smartphone might not seem too difficult on its face, but from rideshare apps to mobile payments, today’s solutions tend to leave a lot more gaps in your life than you might otherwise expect. 

I say all of this because, in some ways, Google appears to be the one smartphone maker seriously thinking about this divide. Sure, the Pixel 11 Pro XL — and its various siblings — all fall into the exact “boring” archetype I’m describing. We’re on the third generation of this design, after all, which itself is an evolved take on the camera bar style initially launched with the Pixel 6 in 2021. Nearly everything new here feels like a software trick that, it’s easy to assume, could be backported to at least some previous Pixels, and the handful of hardware changes you’ll find aren’t all positive.

And yet, Google appears to be attempting to bridge the gap between our always-connected world and the one we left behind. HiLight wants you to turn your phone over, relying on a modernized notification LED in lieu of an always-on display. Magic Capture wants you to take your eyes off the viewfinder so you can get the shot without missing the actual moment. Even the pitch of Gemini Intelligence is designed to anticipate tasks before you actually reach for your phone to begin with.

Whether Google actually pulled this off with the Pixel 11 Pro XL is another story, but there’s certainly something to be said for trying.

	

Hardware and design

We begin, however, with a design that, no doubt, anyone reading this review is all too familiar with. Once again, Google is recycling its Pixel 9 design from 2024, with just a handful of refinements that feel more like change for the sake of change than real stylistic decisions. It’s a few grams lighter than its direct predecessor, but still not as light as the magnet-less Pixel 9 Pro XL — or, for that matter, its closest competitor in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Its chassis is nearly identical to both of Google’s last two swings, though a revised camera bar means you’ll want a new case anyway. Whatever comes next for Pixel, I’m hoping for something a little slimmer and lighter; as it stands, Google’s XL model very much still feels like a brick. A very pretty, very elegant brick, but a brick nonetheless.

I’m a little mixed on my review unit’s Canyon color. As is often the case with Pixels in particular, this shade is less saturated in person than it appears in Google’s online renders, giving the impression of Coral more than anything truly fresh. Yet again, the metal frame on both Pro models remains perfectly polished, designed for attracting smudges, sweat, fingerprints, and scratches. Google is one of the few companies that has yet to fully embrace matte finishes across a flagship portfolio, even as the existence of an all-matte Obsidian model appears to suggest it’s aware of the perks.

Really, aside from an updated slate of colors, it’s the camera bar that gives the game away. Google’s decision to bring back its first uncovered camera bar since the Pixel 6 series can be read as a big swing, considering that model faced some big lens flare issues at the time. I can’t say I’ve seen any more lens flares than usual, thankfully, and all-black look is, admittedly, pretty striking. There’s a reason Google initially chased this look back in 2021, after all, and I think it really works here in a refined, full-circle kind of way.

HiLight

What doesn’t work, though, is the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s new camera flash. Google has seen fit to try to revive notification lights, only modernized for the AI era. The result is HiLight, a terrible name for a terrible product that will make you nostalgic for the freshly-removed temperature sensor you never actually used.

HiLight, at least in its current state, is a waste. It’s a waste of time, space, money, resources, R&D, labor, and LEDs. Only Google, deep in its Gemini mindset, could overcomplicate a notification light — a concept that feels as old as computers themselves — and reduce it to something that can alert you to phone calls from specific contacts. You might be saying, but Will, it also syncs up with Gemini. Not only does that add nothing to the overall experience of actually using Gemini, but by forcing you to turn your phone over, using HiLight means you’ll need to abandon any on-screen context. Zero out of ten, Google. Get an API out the door ASAP, or ditch it on the Pixel 12.

But wait — it gets worse. Google’s new notification light is diffused via a white cover that helps those color LEDs blend and blur together whenever Gemini is active. That’s all well and good, but it comes at the cost of a more usable flashlight. I’ve long thought Google’s LED flashes, particularly in recent years, are pretty mediocre as quick utility flashlights; I don’t mind their warmth, but in comparison to some of its rivals, the throw of the beam was frequently too far to pinpoint specific objects. Worse: prior to Google finally adding a slider to adjust the flashlight brightness, you’d be locked into half of the maximum setting without turning to a third-party app.

So, of course, less than a year after this slider even debuted in a Canary build, Google has seen fit to permanently cut its brightness levels thanks, I assume, to this diffusion layer. It’s possible something else is at play here, such as a smaller LED to make space for the surrounding color lights. Either way, the end result is the same: a frustrating downgrade for anyone who chucked their old flashlight in a drawer back in the 2010s to be preserved for particularly bad storms and power outages. In my view, Pixel 11 Pro buyers should probably throw one more accessory in their shopping cart: a USB-C keychain light.

Am I harping too much on something that, for most users, will simply be a forgotten piece of the phone within a couple of weeks? Perhaps. But I’m also willing to bet that, in 2026, the vast majority of people will use their camera’s flash in lieu of a flashlight far, far more than they do for actual photo-taking. And I have no doubt that some of those people are going to be pretty frustrated by what they find following their upgrade.

Display, specs, and performance

Here’s the good news: the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s display is so good, you’ll probably never want to turn it over to use HiLight anyway. Google’s come a long way since the terrible panel I did my best to ignore nearly a decade ago on the Pixel 2 XL. It’s now rocking a maximum peak brightness of 3,600 nits, along with a more realistic rating of 2,400 nits in high-brightness mode. I’ve carried this thing through no shortage of sunshine-filled late summer walks, and unsurprisingly, had absolutely no issues making out what was on my display at any given time. The bar for flagship screens in direct sunlight was cleared ages ago; everything since has simply been icing on the cake. But what delicious icing it is.

A word of caution, though. Google’s talking a big game about a new display coating that apparently brings “2x scratch resistance” to the device. I’m not trying to call that claim into question, but after a year’s worth of hearing iPhone 17 users talk about the strength of Apple’s Ceramic Shield 2, I might’ve gotten a little cocky. It took less than a week for my unit to pick up a fairly deep scratch in the top-right corner of the display, something I think was caused by it sharing a pocket with a mini USB-C flashlight while doing some home renovations. Would I have had this flashlight in my pocket were HiLight not dimming the camera flash beyond my personal use case? Who’s to say, but at least I brought it full circle.

As usual, Google’s getting some flak for the Pixel 11 Pro’s spec sheet this year, though this time, it’s not just about Tensor. Sure, Tensor G6 — like truly all of its predecessors — leaves something to be desired on sheer raw horsepower if nothing else. I think Google’s basically fixed all of the efficiency hiccups that plagued previous generations; like with the Pixel 10, I didn’t feel this device get more than a little warm during initial setup, and only extended use in direct sunlight has made the chassis feel noticeably warm in my hand since. But I won’t try to pretend there isn’t a group of potential buyers who will once again be let down by this year’s GPU performance.

While I’m sure Google gets plenty of advantage out of controlling as much of its hardware stack as possible — especially as it tries more and more to compete directly against the iPhone — the Tensor experiment continues to feel like it’s failing to achieve true greatness. For whatever advantages Tensor held in the early days on AI performance over Snapdragon, Qualcomm has certainly caught up, all while outperforming Tensor in practically every other metric. And it comes as local AI models seem to have even less to do on mobile than they did just a couple of generations ago. I’m hoping Google eventually gets the message on this; as 9to5’s Damien Wilde said in a recent episode of The Sideload, it’s time for Tensor to have its own Ryzen moment.

Adding fuel to the “who cares about local AI” fire is Google’s decision to drop the base 256GB Pixel 11 Pro models to 12GB of RAM. The company issued 512GB variants to reviewers, which still sport a full 16GB of memory, so it’s tough for me to say how the performance on these downgraded versions match up. However, I’m coming from nearly a full year on the base Pixel 10, so I feel mostly comfortable in saying it shouldn’t make too much of a difference in everyday use for the time being. In seven years though? Your guess is as good as mine.

Software and battery

As I said up top, the Pixel 11 series feels like the start of a big swing from Google to find ways to get people to live in the moment a little more without actually ditching their phone (or, you know, swapping to a minimalist device like Light Phone). Obviously, if this is Google’s strategy moving forward, it’s very early days, and I don’t just say that to kick sand at HiLight again. It really just feels like this is the beginning of a new chapter the company is chasing, and combined with new enhancements to Digital Wellbeing coming… eventually, it’s an agenda I’m all about.

That said, I’m hard-pressed to find anything in this space I’d call a complete success. I’ve seen Proactive Assistance — Google’s update to last year’s middling Magic Cue — activate just once on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, over a list of potential birthday dessert recipes stored in Keep. Gemini prompted me to “Shop groceries,” but tapping that action simply created a prompt to order the desserts as if they were, you know, actual ingredients and not “Banoffee Pudding.” Were I more of a Google Messages user, I’m sure I’d have more to say about this tool, but unfortunately, my reliance on third-party chat apps is one of the more European things about me. Some of the non-messaging tools, like location-based suggestions within At a Glance, also have yet to show up on my device.

I continue to be more or less underwhelmed by Gemini in general. It’s perfectly fine for really run-of-the-mill searches or prompts — you know, spaces in which it can mostly paraphrase Wikipedia — but venture off a relatively narrow path and I inevitably find myself getting frustrated. A search for a specific brand of craft root beer in the greater Western New York area, which I thought would be a relatively simple task, drove me in circles until I finally just texted a friend who’d been to the actual store in person. Really, Gemini’s big advantage right now is just how baked in it is to the Pixel experience, but I’d be lying if I said it doesn’t feel like all of this would be at least a little better if Gemini 3.5 Pro wasn’t months late.

Basically, today, Google’s idea of saving you time or keeping you connected to the physical world around you mostly exists in advertisements and hypothetical situations. There are spaces where this isn’t true — check out Daniel Bader’s extended thoughts on Magic Capture for a perfect example — but if, like me, you were sold by the pitch of a device you can easily ignore without having to create an entirely new minimalist experience for yourself, just know that reality hasn’t arrived quite yet.

These sorts of features on Niagara are exactly the strategies Google should be looking towards to refresh its launcher.

I’d also argue Google could take more steps in this direction without having to wait for future models with improved AI performance simply by giving its launcher a (in my opinion) much-needed makeover. For all of the Pixel’s promises towards being “proactive” or “predictive,” I’m genuinely surprised we haven’t seen a rethinking of the traditional grid of icons and widgets on your home screen. I look at something like Niagara, which has intelligent media widgets or in-line notifications for your most-used apps, and I wonder why Google hasn’t thought to build similar experiences into the Pixel’s launcher. The closest tool is probably Gemini’s Daily Brief, which mostly exists to try and pull contextual data from places like Gmail into a single list. It’s… fine, but it’s not quite the leap into the future I’d be hoping for — nor is it actually built into the launcher.

While the Pixel 11 Pro XL is undoubtedly behind today’s true battery champs — I wouldn’t say I had difficulty in killing this device the way I did, say, the OnePlus 15 — I never found myself stressing about whether I’d make it to the end of the day. Usually, I was heading to bed with about 40% left in the tank. Keep in mind I spend most of my day on Wi-Fi, but even on days where I was out of the house for longer stretches, I never really felt the need to make sure I was charged up. As unscientific as it may sound, if you’re an average mixed-use smartphone user like myself, you’ll likely experience very minimal battery anxiety.

Camera

If there’s one space where I think even those with relatively recent Pixel devices might be tempted to upgrade, it’s the camera. Google has packed the Pixel 11 Pro XL with a refreshed main sensor and an upgraded 5x telephoto lens that now supports 120x Super Res Zoom. While it’s still absolutely susceptible to creating images that look like AI-generated slop, Super Res Zoom is also capable of capturing a shockingly accurate image of a bird that barely appears within the same shot taken at 1x. It’s impressive, even if you probably won’t want to max it out super often.

That main 1/1.3″ sensor sounds familiar on paper, but it’s allowed Google to bring forth Instant Night Sight, a long-awaited upgrade to the Pixel’s low-light mode that, believe it or not, has been around for nearly a decade now. I can’t speak to whether Google’s quoted 4.5x speed improvement is fully accurate or not, but in practice, it’s certainly faster.

If there’s one thing I’d love to see Google work on for the Pixel 12, it’s a more accurate Night Sight. While the speed in which the Pixel 11 Pro XL can capture and enhance a low-light image into something easily viewable is no doubt impressive, it still frequently defaults to an photo that goes way too far in brightening scenes that probably should, you know, look like nighttime. In one example, a fairly dim image of my cat Linus hanging out in our living room ended up looking like the overhead kitchen light was on behind him, which… it wasn’t. The second shot, which forced me to dial back the exposure manually, is much closer to reality without being too dim.

I could probably go on for 1,000 words about Camera Looks, my favorite Pixel 11 feature and my favorite addition to the Pixel’s camera in quite some time, except I already did. Here’s the short version: Despite some relatively-minor UX decisions that left me scratching my head, this is exactly what I’ve been hoping Google would build into the Pixel’s camera app since at least the Pixel 7. The customizable defaults are great starting points, and shooting with the more personality-driven modes like Editorial or Digi is so fun.

Actually, fun might be the best word to describe Camera Looks. It’s really brought a sense of joy and experimentation to the Pixel 11’s camera system that I’ve sorely missed through the Tensor era, and I hope Google keeps adding to this experience for generations to come. But man, what a bummer this isn’t getting backported to older hardware.

Some minor complaints aside, though, this really is the happiest I’ve been with a Pixel camera in ages. I haven’t felt the need to tweak a shot in Photos after the fact in the two weeks I’ve been using this device, and I don’t expect that to change any time soon. It’s nice to see Google giving more freedom to its photographer fans after half a decade of safe, sterile, contrast-free images.

Conclusion

Google’s Pixel 11 pitch as a more intelligent evolution of the smartphone experience you already know might’ve been a little too early for its own good, but I can see the vision forming. While I remain a skeptic of agentic AI applications ever radically shifting my interactions with Android, I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t a little refreshing — or sobering, even? — to see a tech giant like Google at least acknowledging the growing cry for a break, even if leaning into AI is likely exactly what that audience doesn’t want. It’s an interesting dilemma, and I’m excited to see how the Pixel series continues to tackle it, both through software updates and future hardware refreshes.

Today, though, the Pixel 11 Pro XL mostly exists as yet another phone. Its big aspirations towards a more peaceful future — HiLight, Proactive Assistant — mostly fall flat in practice, all while revealing all sorts of missed opportunities to really rethink the modern approach to smartphones. Then again, there’s very little here that can’t be improved in the months and years to come; slow and steady usually wins the race, after all.

Potential aside, the Pixel 11 Pro XL you can actually buy right now is quite good for all but the most demanding of users. It’s a big, bold, bright display paired with solid battery life, excellent quality-of-life improvements like stronger Pixelsnap magnets (a feature you still won’t find on most other Android phones, Samsung), and — from my perspective — a definitive claim to the camera throne, at least here in the US. As has become tradition with Google’s hardware refreshes, there’s very little to truly dislike here, especially from a core experience perspective.

While we’re expecting a much bigger swing next year with the Pixel 12 — assuming RAMageddon hasn’t derailed Google’s confirmed design cycle — if you’re ready for a new smartphone right now, I wouldn’t hold back from picking up the Pixel 11 Pro XL. It might not be a total success in pulling off its vision for the future of mobile, but that can’t prevent it from being a reliable daily driver in the present. And if this is a cap on the era of Pixel that began with the Pixel 6, it’s certainly an ending to be celebrated.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and is available now.

title: Google’s next Pixel Fold reportedly adopting the same crease-less display as Apple
snippet: We’re still a few days out from the debut of Apple’s first iPhone foldable which, as many have expected for years, will have a crease-less display. According to a new report, Google’s Pixel 12 Pro Fold will be adopting the same technology as Apple’s foldable. more…
fullText:
We’re still a few days out from the debut of Apple’s first iPhone foldable which, as many have expected for years, will have a crease-less display. According to a new report, Google’s Pixel 12 Pro Fold will be adopting the same technology as Apple’s foldable.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is, as we’ve mentioned, a perfectly fine foldable. But as brands such as Oppo, Honor, and most recently Samsung have gone all-in on crease-less displays, Google’s foldable is noticeably behind. 

Review: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold just barely keeps up

According to a new report, Google plans a major upgrade on the Pixel 12 Pro Fold, and they’re not the only ones. The Elec reports that Google, Oppo, and Vivo are all working with Samsung Display to adopt dual-UTG (ultra-thin glass) displays for their next-gen foldables. It’s the same tech apparently set to be used on Apple’s first iPhone foldable. 

Samsung Display and partners would be building out the display and UTG assembly to the specs of each device. This sees one UTG layer above the display, with a second layer underneath and supporting the OLED panel. Samsung achieved its crease-less display using a special titanium plate under the OLED panel, while Oppo says it filled in the area of the crease using liquid 3D printing to create an even surface along with thicker glass.

	

The report mentions that Oppo and Vivo will both have releases in the first half of 2027, while Google’s next foldable will come in the second half – probably in August, as per the usual schedule.

title: Pixel Now Playing update brings interface tweaks
snippet: The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks. more…
fullText:
The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks.

When tapping on an identified song’s three-dot button, Now Playing slides up a bottom sheet. This replaces the floating menu and is better for one-handed navigation.

You’ll see track information with side-by-side buttons for Share, Add to favorites, and Remove from history. This is followed by a button to play the song and any shortcuts specific to your connected music service.

Meanwhile, the Favorites tab now includes dates and times like the History feed. There are also icon and spacing tweaks in Now Playing Settings.

	

The redesigned Now Playing launched in March, while Google in April reintroduced the “Tap to see what’s playing” shortcut on the lockscreen.

Version 2026.08.27.x of Pixel Now Playing is widely rolling out via the Google Play Store.

This follows last month’s updates to Pixel Journal that added more tools and Screenshots (extra filter options), as well as new icons for Google Calculator, Clock, Pixel Magnifier, Recorder, and Weather.

title: Sept. 2026 Android Drop: Find Hub ‘Remembered’ list, Motion Assist, & Keep in Google Messages
snippet: Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features.

Find Hub Remembered

Find Hub and Gemini can now keep track of things that don’t have a tracker tag on them. You can now tell “Gemini to remember where you placed important items.” For example, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer,” with the ability to add a photo. 

The location will be saved to a new “Remembered” tab in the Find Hub app. You can also ask Gemini for its location with a voice command. This is rolling out on Android 16+.

Motion Assist

Motion Assist on Android 17+ will help reduce motion sickness with a subtle bubble overlay on your screen that moves with the vehicle. This is “designed to help bridge the gap between what your eyes see and the movement of your ride.”

	

You can customize the color, shape, and opacity. There’s also an option to have the color and shape change every few seconds.

Android can enable Motion Assist automatically when movement in a car, bus, or train is detected, while there’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut.

Gemini Live Guided Vision

Gemini Live is adding Guided Vision to offer verbal “descriptions of what’s in front of you.” Use cases include “reading fine print on a food label, ordering from a menu in a low-lit restaurant, or locating household objects.”

If your camera isn’t lined up, voice feedback will guide you to reframe, pan across a space, or center an object so you get the answers you need. 

Guided Vision is available as an Accessibility shortcut or via the TalkBack menu. This is “coming soon to phones running Android 9+ in countries where Gemini is available.”

Google Messages Keep integration

Following the wide rollout of Chat themes, Google Messages is adding Google Keep integration. This lets you “share and update grocery lists or vacation notes right inside your chat.”

A “Create list” suggestion and ‘plus’ menu shortcut will bring up a sheet that lets you start creating. Once done, the list will appear inline as a shared note. This integration is rolling out starting today.

title: Ryan Reynolds’ new Apple TV spy movie is a winner, reviews here
snippet: Apple TV kicks off its big fall lineup this week with Mayday, a new Ryan Reynolds film that’s part buddy comedy, part action spy thriller. And the first reviews say the movie’s a winner. more…
fullText:
Apple TV kicks off its big fall lineup this week with Mayday, a new Ryan Reynolds film that’s part buddy comedy, part action spy thriller. And the first reviews say the movie’s a winner.

Mayday reviews praise the film’s action, humor, and lead duo’s chemistry

Apple TV is best known for its shows, and has great ones airing now like Ted Lasso and sci-fi hits Dark Matter and Silo. But movies on Apple TV are on the rise too.

title: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym
snippet: GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories. With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios. more…
fullText:
GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

GymKit, no Apple Watch required

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

As a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

iPhone and AirPods have become more like an Apple Watch

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods users a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

AirPods heart-rate permission also matters. You can manage it in Settings under your AirPods settings and privacy options. I had turned it off, mostly as a theoretical battery-saving move, but this test convinced me to turn it back on. AirPods Pro 3 can also work with Apple Watch to provide the best available heart-rate data.

GymKit on iPhone with AirPods is a great addition to Apple’s Fitness ecosystem

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics. That’s a neat upgrade, and it makes Apple’s broader Fitness strategy feel more complete.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so popular that Samsung is stealing parts from next year’s phones just to make more
snippet: Samsung has a hit on its hands with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, to the point where the company is taking parts production from its 2027 smartphones just to meet demand for the foldable. more…
fullText:
Samsung has a hit on its hands with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, to the point where the company is taking parts production from its 2027 smartphones just to meet demand for the foldable.

ZDNet Korea reports that Samsung has run into a wall when it comes to boosting Galaxy Z Fold 8 production, with demand for the foldable far outpacing initial supply. Shipping delays were seen immediately after launch, and Samsung even set out to produce one million more units. 

The problem Samsung has run into, the report brings out, is around Display Driver ICs (DDIs). This specific part is built by a Taiwan-based semiconductor foundry, UMC, on a 22nm process with the partner having “reached its limit” around building these parts. As a result, Samsung is prioritizing DDI volume that was already secured for 2027 products and shifting that to boosting production of the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Samsung isn’t directly using parts designed for other devices here, though, as the DDI is built specifically for each individual phone model. It’s the production of these parts that is being shifted around, which is still a major change on Samsung’s part. Samsung has also requested a “super hot run” – i.e. “express service” – for the Fold 8’s DDIs in order to meet demand. 

	

This comes as the Fold 8 is partially out of stock on Samsung.com in the US, and the foldable continues to contribute to a rapidly growing foldable market. Omdia this week reports that foldable shipments will double by 2028 to the tune of around 36 million units.

title: iOS 27 gives Apple Pay its best upgrade in years with redesign
snippet: iOS 27 introduces several improvements for Apple Pay, including a fully overhauled checkout flow that’s the service’s best upgrade in years. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 introduces several improvements for Apple Pay, including a fully overhauled checkout flow that’s the service’s best upgrade in years.

New design for Apple Pay checkout screen in iOS 27 is better in every way

Apple Pay checkout screen: new (left) vs old (right) 

Apple Pay has become one of the most popular payment methods in the world. It’s so universally available that even Walmart finally gave in and added support.

And with its popularity, any significant change Apple implements could be risky—especially a design change like iOS 27 brings.

Apple Pay has a new design in iOS 27 when checking out in apps or on the web. And I’m happy to report it’s a fantastic upgrade that’s better in every way.

The old checkout design had a couple main faults:

Switching cards wasn’t intuitive

Onscreen data wasn’t easy to parse at a glance

Despite years of using Apple Pay, I’ve still never gotten used to the historic method for switching cards. I always tap near the top where the active card is displayed, only to load the address screen and have to go back to find the actual card selection menu.

iOS 27 fixes that. When you first open the checkout interface, you’ll see additional cards on either side of your default card, indicating you can swipe between them to switch. It’s quick, easy, and far more intuitive.

Additionally, iOS 27 shows more information onscreen at once, and uses colorful icons to denote relevant info like shipping method and address, billing address, and more.

The redesign makes it much easier to verify everything is accurate and as it should be. Then you can quickly double click to pay with the assurance there are no mistakes.

Changing the design for something used by millions, and with real-world consequences for errors, is a tall task. But in my opinion, Apple has done a fantastic job with iOS 27’s Apple Pay revamp.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

RugOne’s Xsnap 7 Pro comes with both an IP68 and IP69K rating, meaning the rugged phone can survive intense water blasts and complete submersion for up to 30 minutes. But what really sets the Xsnap 7 Pro apart from everything else on the market is that one of its three rear cameras can be removed and used as a standalone action cam. It made its debut at MWC 2026 earlier this year but is launching through Kickstarter on September 7th for €799 (around $930) in limited quantities, followed by a global release in October for $999.

The Xsnap 7 Pro’s detachable camera module isn’t quite as a capable as the DJI Osmo Nano or the Insta360 Go Ultra that both record at 4K. Its video capabilities max out at 2.7K at up to 30fps captured through a 133-degree ultrawide field-of-view lens. Video is processed by distortion correction algorithms to keep subjects looking natural, while software stabilization helps smooth out footage even when the camera is flipped 360 degrees, RugOne claims.

The action cam’s battery keeps it recording for up to 40 minutes, which can be extended to up to 800 minutes when repeatedly docked and charged using the phone’s own 9,300mAh battery. The camera’s 64GB of built-in storage can hold up to eight hours of 1080p footage, but videos can be transferred to the Xsnap 7 Pro’s 512GB of storage every time it’s docked. Waterproofing for the camera is slightly better than the phone, as it can be used to a depth of 5 meters instead of just 2.

The Xsnap 7 Pro is powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 5G processor with 12GB of RAM and ships with Android 16 with upgrades to up to Android 20 promised. It’s got a 6.67-inch 120Hz AMOLED screen that can be used as a wireless preview screen for the action camera at distances of up to 160 feet. Alongside the detachable camera, the Xsnap 7 pro includes a 32MP selfie camera on the front plus a stabilized 50MP main camera on the back, alongside a 64MP night vision camera boosted with infrared LEDs.

title: IFA Finally Showed Me a Smart Answer for Home Radiator Heating
snippet: Sonoff arrived at IFA with a much-needed smart solution for radiators and I’m very happy.
fullText:
I’ve covered the many ways smart thermostats can convert your home to a well-heated haven and how quickly they can pay for themselves through energy savings, but there’s one glaring issue. Almost all smart thermostats are designed only for central hubs and forced air heating/cooling. Imagine my relief when Sonoff showed up at IFA 2026 with a smart alternative.

Read more: The Weirdest and Wackiest Tech We Found at IFA 2026

At last, I’ve found an alternative, thanks to Sonoff’s announcement of its latest TRV Smart Thermostatic Radiator Valve. It’s designed to fit on the valve pipe of a traditional home radiator, screwing in place and connecting to Wi-Fi to provide app insights and a full suite of control options. It’s available right now on the Sonoff website for $35 and supports both Celsius and Fahrenheit.

It’s difficult to find up-to-date smart radiator solutions in the IS, let alone everything Sonoff is offering here. The valve lets you adjust between several temperature plans and uses an IPS color screen to show temperature and settings at a glance. Its app also offers low-battery alerts so you can recharge it, as well as important reminders for frost protection, anti-calcification maintenance and even connections to window sensors that can automatically stop heating when windows are opened. There’s even a child lock to keep little fingers from messing up your heating schedule.

This combination of features is exactly what people need if they live in homes that primarily use radiators, have radiators in addition to central heating, or use radiators only in certain spots, like a finished basement. It offers the same savings potential and convenience as standard smart thermostats, plus some features tailored specifically for radiators.

Since I don’t have radiators in my home, I can’t easily test this smart valve out. I’ll have to ask other CNET editors if one of their rooms has a radiator they could test in so we can get real-world results, but everything looks promising here.

Are you more of a radiant floor heat home? Sonoff has you covered, too

Sonoff also has a smart upgrade for those with heated flooring. Sonoff

Many newer homes have a different kind of heating technology, radiant flooring heating, popular in bathrooms and homes with certain kinds of wood flooring. If you’re interested in smart additions to this kind of radiant heating, Sonoff brought good news to IFA for you, too. 

Sonoff also announced a Thermostat Core, designed to fit standard hydronic underfloor heating systems. It outfits floor heating with complete app controls, scheduling options and connection options with Sonoff temperature sensors, so floor heating can respond to the current temperature of a specific room. It sports a presence-activated screen, frost protection and other synergies similar to the radiator valve, too.

I don’t currently have pricing information for the Thermostat Core, but when I find out the details, I’ll let you know.

While I’m most excited about the smart heating, I’d be remiss not to mention that Sonoff announced several other smart products at IFA. It showed off an indoor siren and, most notably, a window security cam. Eufy also showed up with a window camera at IFA, so it’s apparently a new home security trend. Wyze got in the game much earlier this year with its own window security cam, and you can see what I thought about it here. These unique, covered cams fit directly on windows and are particularly useful for apartments and similar spots.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma

title: I Took the Pixel 11 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Around Delhi, and I Know Which Phone Camera’s the Best for Me
snippet: The Pixel 11 Pro debuted this summer with some new camera enhancements, and I wanted to see how it shapes up against the iPhone 17 Pro ahead of Apple’s Sept. 9 event.
fullText:
Google is promising “incredible camera upgrades” with its new $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro, but with a rumored iPhone 18 Pro likely debuting on Wednesday, I wanted to see how the phone’s photography shapes up against the iPhone 17 Pro. 

Google touts a few enhancements that could make a difference, including better dynamic range on its wide camera and 30% higher light sensitivity on its zoom sensor. And those boosts could improve photos, even if the 11 Pro’s camera hardware is largely similar to last year’s 10 Pro — featuring a 50-megapixel wide lens, a 48-megapixel ultrawide and a 48-megapixel telephoto with a 5x optical zoom.

Apple’s iPhone 17 Pro also has a mighty camera system even after a year on the market, with 48-megapixel wide, ultrawide and telephoto cameras. The telephoto camera has a 4x optical zoom that can achieve an 8x magnification with Apple’s software. 

Google Pixel 11 Pro’s camera system includes a 50-megapixel wide lens, a 48-megapixel ultrawide and a 48-megapixel telephoto with a 5x optical zoom.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

The two phones also offer their own versions of color profiles to help you add your creative style to the photos rather than relying on the default looks. However, for this comparison, I resorted to default processing across the lenses. Google tends to brighten the shadows, whereas Apple leans toward a more natural tone.

I took both phones around Delhi to see how they perform in a variety of environments, including a few beautiful monuments in Lodhi Garden that provided plenty of well-lit and shadowy areas to see how Apple and Google’s best phone cameras show these places off. While phone photography can vary in all kinds of environments and is subjective, here’s how I felt each phone performed in capturing fine details and colors.

Google Pixel 11 Pro

Apple iPhone 17 Pro

Main

50-megapixel; 1/1.3-inch sensor with OIS; 25mm

48-megapixel;1/1.28-inch sensor with OIS, 24mm

Telephoto

48-megapixel; 1/1.95-inch sensor with 5x optical zoom and OIS, 120mm

48-megapixel; 1/2.55-inch sensor with 4x optical zoom and OIS, 100mm

Ultrawide

48-megapixel; 123-degree field-of-view

48-megapixel; 120-degree field-of-view

Main camera

Left: Pixel 11 Pro image. Right: iPhone 17 Pro image.

In overcast conditions, Apple’s colors look more accurate to the scene, but the Pixel 11 Pro better exposed the overall frame. It delivered a better dynamic range, and if you look at the leaves on the trees, you’ll find that Google was able to capture more details in the shadows. The iPhone 17 Pro Max shot looks less lively in comparison.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro. Right: iPhone 17 Pro.

Both phones take decent portrait shots, but nothing like what you’d get from a Vivo, Xiaomi or Oppo’s Ultra models available in international markets. Those phones are still leagues ahead. In these shots, the Pixel 11 Pro has a pink-ish hue, but I still prefer it over the iPhone because my skin tone looks more natural here. The Apple portrait shot looks too processed for my taste. While these were shot on the main camera, Google is finally allowing Portraits to be taken using its telephoto camera.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro. Right: iPhone 17 Pro.

Both phones are capable of taking macro photos. The Pixel 11 Pro captured more textures on the flower petal while focusing on the water droplets. In comparison, the iPhone shot looks smoother, but I like Apple’s bokeh here. It looks more pleasant.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro. Right: iPhone 17 Pro.

I chose this frame because it transitions from dark to light and features a distant subject. The difference in colors is more apparent in 2x digital zoom. Apple leans on the warmer side, while Pixel has a comparatively cool color temperature. Both phones were able to capture a good amount of detail and retain the clarity at 1x.

Telephoto camera

The Pixel 11 Pro offers 5x optical zoom, whereas the iPhone 17 Pro offers 4x optical zoom. A black cat in a dark environment with backlight is one of the challenging scenes, but I couldn’t get the exact same frame because my furry friend decided to change its pose.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro at 5x zoom. Right: iPhone 17 Pro at 4x zoom.

The Pixel 11 Pro managed to capture more details and comparatively accurate colors. The cat’s yellow eyes are sharper on the Google phone, while you can also see the details on its fur. The iPhone, on the other hand, struggled with clarity — you do see the cat and the bricks, but I feel like the Pixel was able to make out more distinct details like the cat’s nose and the different shades of color on the building.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro at 5x zoom. Right: iPhone 17 Pro at 4x zoom.

I put my friend in a similar frame, and both phones captured the skin tone well but had some sort of halo effect — possibly from the light source behind my subject — that made the shot look unnatural. In terms of colors, the iPhone got my friend’s hair color right, while the Pixel’s cooler tone changed the shade of green.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro at 5x zoom. Right: iPhone 17 Pro at 4x zoom.

I prefer the Pixel 11 Pro shot in this comparison because of better contrast and more accurate skin tone. If you look at the building, you’ll notice that the iPhone 17 Pro photo is less sharp and doesn’t have the same amount of detail, including the texture in the green and pink parts of the monument. It is more pronounced in the Pixel shot.

Ultrawide camera

Left: Pixel 11 Pro ultrawide camera. Right: iPhone 17 Pro ultrawide camera.

In ultrawide angle too, the Pixel 11 Pro continues to better expose the shadows in darker areas of the photo. It is comparatively brighter, too, and I’d pick it over the iPhone shot. I’ve included the 1x shot here for context — the colors remain consistent across main and ultrawide cameras on both phones.

Left: Pixel 11 Pro at 1x zoom. Right: iPhone 17 Pro at 1x zoom.

The photography experience

For what I value in a photo, I preferred Google’s Pixel 11 Pro over Apple’s iPhone 17 Pro in most of the scenes I tested. I felt the Pixel 11 Pro’s photos had more contrast, brighter visuals, and I felt like it delivered sharper results in zoom shots. All of this equated to more lively, social media-ready shots.

I will caveat that I am not a fan of the Pixel 11 Pro’s camera app nor the Google Photos app — I find menu options like Camera Looks are buried in the viewfinder, and the Google Photos app puts too much emphasis on resurfacing throwback photos, especially when I’m in the middle of finding something different. It is cluttered and distracting.

	

			

Apple’s iPhone 17 Pro is still a very good option. I feel it offers a more accurate representation of the scenes I captured, even though I prefer the photos the Pixel 11 Pro created. I like how Google’s phone created brighter scenes, even if that was through more digital processing. 

As we look forward to the iPhone 18 Pro, I hope Apple’s next phone steps up its zoom photos — perhaps with a bigger telephoto sensor — to better compete against the zoomed photos I captured with the Pixel 11 Pro.

title: Google Health 5.07 rolling out with better manual logging, maps, & more
snippet: Google Health 5.07 is rolling out on Android and iOS with meaningful updates to manual workout logging and a handful of bug fixes. more…
fullText:
Google Health 5.07 is rolling out on Android and iOS with meaningful updates to manual workout logging and a handful of bug fixes.

Version 5.07 lets you manually enter more metrics, with additions appearing in “workout summaries more quickly once you’ve made them.” There’s also a sizable update to map performance. The update is still rolling out on Android and widely available on iOS today.

The full list of improvements and fixes is organized into three categories:

Activity and Fitness Updates

	

Improved Manual Workout Logging: We’ve made three updates for users who log exercises manually. First, you can now add and adjust more metrics when logging an exercise manually. Your edits will also show up in the workout summaries more quickly once you’ve made them. And finally, you can now log more metrics when switching from a pool to open swim exercise.

Maps: We’ve continued to improve the maps experience, with faster loading times, and smoother rendering and adjustments. We’ve also fixed an issue where maps were occasionally missing when using your phone to track a running, biking, or walking session.

Running Distance Totals: Trail runs and incline runs now count toward your Running Distance totals.

Weight Tracking Updates

Weight Graph: We’ve recalibrated the graph’s dynamic minimum and maximum range so your weight trends and changes are easier to view at a glance. 

Health Connect Updates

We’ve fixed an issue that caused some Android users to lose their connection with Health Connect. If you were impacted, you’ll now see Health Connect listed in the Partner Apps section of the Connections screen.

title: Sony’s new ULT Tower party speakers start at $450
snippet: Sony has announced new additions to its ULT Tower party speaker lineup, now offering options that are much more affordable. more…
fullText:
Sony has announced new additions to its ULT Tower party speaker lineup, now offering options that are much more affordable.

The Sony ULT Tower collection kicked off back in 2024 with a pricey but powerful $1,200 speaker. The ULT Tower 9 launched earlier this year with a smaller, but still pricey $900 package. These speakers are designed with parties in mind, delivering music on a much larger scale than a traditional Bluetooth speaker.

Now, Sony is expanding the lineup.

Three new Sony ULT Tower party speakers are launching in September, starting with the most affordable of the bunch, the ULT Tower 5. This is the most compact of the bunch – it’s not exactly small – but Sony says it still delivers “impressive bass and sound pressure.” Like the rest of the lineup, it also features four sound profiles, including: 

	

ULT1: Enhances deep bass for a rich, low-frequency sound that makes your heart tremble.

ULT2: Boosts even greater power, delivering body-shaking bass and strong sound pressure.

FLAT: Reproduces music exactly as intended, delivering a true-to-source listening experience.

LIVE: Recreates the spacious feel of a live performance while preserving vocal clarity.

ULT Tower 5 starts at $450, with the whole lineup on Sony’s website, Amazon, and more.

The whole lineup also supports wireless audio alongside XLR, USB, and Line inputs, as well as having a microphone input too. Multiple speakers can also be set up in a stereo pair.

Meanwhile, ULT Tower 7 offers more power and volume, as well as adding 360-degree audio at $650.

ULT Tower Max is the last option debuting this month, jumping up to the top of the lineup at $1,500. This monstrous party speaker has three woofers (two front and one back-facing) as well as four tweeters, 360-degree sound, and “a high-powered amplifier.”

title: Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is a MacBook Neo competitor starting at $699
snippet: Lenovo is taking on the MacBook Neo with a colorful new laptop – the IdeaPad Vibe. more…
fullText:
Lenovo is taking on the MacBook Neo with a colorful new laptop – the IdeaPad Vibe.

Announced at Lenovo Innovation World ahead of IFA, the Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is squarely aimed at Apple’s most affordable and incredibly popular MacBook Neo, and it puts up a good fight on paper. The laptop can be outfitted with either a 14-inch or 15-inch OLED display and measures in at 14.9mm thick and from 2.87lbs. Thicker and bigger than Apple’s laptop, but not all that much heavier, at least in its starting weight. Lenovo says the Vibe will be available in both plastic and metal variations.

Metal
Plastic

It sure looks the part, though, with Lenovo teaming up with Pantone to offer 7 different color options for the IdeaPad Vibe including:

Dreamy Violet: a muted violet shade layered with inviting depth that inspires serenity, bringing a sense of comfort wherever it goes.

Spicy Gold: A rich golden yellow that blends warmth and energy, creating a confident, welcoming feeling.

Zen Green: A nature inspired green hue that evokes a sense of balance, harmony, and encourages a slower pace.

Chill Blue: An icy blue with a crisp modern vibe that stimulates refreshing clarity and an effortless fresh start energy.

Radiant Coral: Warm and uplifting with an optimistic orange boost that brings friendliness and positivity wherever it goes.

Moody Blue: Expressing credibility and confidence, a deep blue hue conveying refined elegance.

Lowkey Grey: A timeless grey projecting strength, stability, and understated sophistication.

The keyboard also features interchangeable keycaps so you can customize the look with some fun color combinations.

	

These are all metal versions

Pretty colors only matter so much, though, and Lenovo has stacked this laptop with a pretty enticing setup. You get a pair of USB-A ports, an HDMI port, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and even a microSD card reader. There’s a 5MP webcam (with physical privacy cover), an optional keyboard backlight, and an optional touchscreen on the 15-inch size.

But what’s under the hood?

You can pick between an AMD Ryzen AI 400 chip or a Qualcomm Snapdragon X chip. The AMD model supports up to 32GB of RAM which can be upgraded by the end user. Configurations also include up to 1TB of storage, also upgradable and featuring dual slots. The Snapdragon version supports up to 24GB of RAM and, while the storage is still upgradable, the RAM is not. Lenovo says to also expect an Intel version in the future.

The Lenovo IdeaPad Vibe is launching in two initial waves. AMD models will be available in October, with Snapdragon to follow in November. Both will start at $699.99, matching the price of the MacBook Neo since Apple’s RAM-induced price hike. 

Meanwhile, Lenovo is also introducing the IdeaCentre AIO I which is an all-in-one desktop computer with a 24-inch or 27-inch display, similar colors to the Vibe, and a price starting at $939. It will also be available starting in November.

title: Brydge announces color-matched keyboards for the entry-level iPad
snippet: Brydge, the Apple accessory company that came back from the dead back in 2023, has just announced a new set of colour-matched keyboards for the entry-level iPad. While Apple offers the iPad itself in a choice of four colours, the Magic Keyboard for it is only available in white. That’s what prompted Brydge to launch its latest lineup … more…
fullText:
Brydge, the Apple accessory company that came back from the dead back in 2023, has just announced a new set of colour-matched keyboards for the entry-level iPad.

While Apple offers the iPad itself in a choice of four colours, the Magic Keyboard for it is only available in white. That’s what prompted Brydge to launch its latest lineup … 

The 11-inch base model iPad is available in a choice of silver, blue, pink, and yellow. Brydge is now offering what it describes as a premium aluminium keyboard to match each of the four colours.

The idea is simple: you chose your favorite iPad color. Now your keyboard can match it. Most aluminum iPad keyboards are offered in traditional neutral finishes. Brydge 11.0 takes a different approach, using color-matched anodized aluminum designed to match the iPad’s own Blue, Pink, Yellow and Silver finishes […] creating a setup that looks like it belongs together, rather than an iPad with a keyboard simply added on.

The company says that it offers the build quality and features Brydge products are known for. This includes  a solid aluminium construction, a full-size backlit keyboard with 1.3mm of travel, an all-glass multi-touch trackpad supporting all iPadOS gestures, and strong magnets to hold the iPad in place. Bluetooth automatically reconnects when the case is opened.

Battery life is said to be up to three months without the backlight and a total of 40 hours’ use with the backlight on. It is recharged via USB-C.

Known as the Brydge 11.0, the keyboard is compatible with the iPad (10th generation) and iPad (A16), and costs $159. This compares to $249 for Apple’s Magic Keyboard Folio. The lineup is set to go on sale on the company’s website and official Amazon store around the middle of the month.

title: Today is Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO, John Ternus takes over tomorrow
snippet: After 15 years at the helm, today is officially Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO. In April, Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO on September 1, with John Ternus set to take the reins. Cook, of course, isn’t going away completely. Instead, he’s set to become executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors. more…
fullText:
After 15 years at the helm, today is officially Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO. In April, Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO on September 1, with John Ternus set to take the reins.

Cook, of course, isn’t going away completely. Instead, he’s set to become executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors.

Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO 

Cook became Apple’s CEO in 2011, two months before Steve Jobs passed away. Ternus, meanwhile, joined Apple in 2001 as a member of the company’s Product Design team. He moved up the ranks quickly and was formally promoted to senior vice president of Hardware Engineering in January of 2021.

In a report over the weekend, Bloomberg reiterated that Cook’s focus as executive chairman will see him managing Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government.

Cook will serve as Apple’s executive chairman. He’s told Ternus that he’ll keep managing the company’s relationships with President Donald Trump and the Chinese government, and that he’s eager to handle any other tasks his successor deems necessary. While Cook has talked about plans to take up more outdoor activities and spend time at his vacation home in Palm Springs, he’s also told staffers the company will remain his No. 1 priority, because he “can’t imagine it any other way.”

When he becomes CEO, Ternus is expected to take Tim Cook’s current office, Bloomberg says. The Information has reported that Cook’s executive assistant will stay on and work for Ternus.

Apple held a farewell dinner for Cook at Apple Park last week, according to reports. This included “hours of tributes from Ternus, Laurene Powell Jobs, and other current and former Apple executives.” OneRepublic, one of Cook’s favorite bands, also performed at the event.

The transition comes ahead of Apple’s “Surprise and shine” special event, which will take place on Wednesday, September 9. Cook will not be featured in the event. Instead, it will be spearheaded by Ternus. During the event, Apple is expected to unveil the foldable iPhone Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro, new Apple Watch models, and more.

In recent weeks, Apple has made a wave of unpopular announcements, including raising prices on most of its hardware products (but not iPhone), as well as subscription services including Apple TV, Apple Music, and Apple One. This should set the stage for Ternus to take over and focus on kicking off what’s been described as Apple’s most ambitious product cycle ever.

Are you excited to see Ternus take over as Apple CEO tomorrow? What changes do you hope he makes? How would you grade Cook’s tenure? Let us know down in the comments.

title: When is Apple releasing new AirPods?
snippet: Apple’s AirPods lineup is stronger than ever, but there are already rumors about what’s coming next. Here’s everything we know so far about when Apple will release new AirPods. more…
fullText:
Apple’s AirPods lineup is stronger than ever, but there are already rumors about what’s coming next. Here’s everything we know so far about when Apple will release new AirPods.

Apple’s current AirPods lineup

Here is Apple’s AirPods lineup as it stands today:

AirPods 4 (currently on sale for $99)

AirPods 4 with Active Noise Cancellation (currently on sale for $149)

AirPods Pro 3 (currently on sale for $99)

AirPods Max 2 (currently on sale for $479)

When is Apple releasing new AirPods? 

AirPods with cameras

The biggest change coming to Apple’s AirPods lineup is a new version of AirPods with built-in cameras.

This pair of AirPods will have a camera in both the left and the right earbuds. The cameras, however, aren’t designed for photo and video capture. Instead, they will be used in conjunction with Siri to provide context for the environment around you. Bloomberg has described them as “the eyes” for Siri.

For example, while looking at food ingredients, you could ask your AirPods what to make for dinner or for specific nutritional information. They might also integrate with other apps on your iPhone, such as Reminders and Maps, to provide environmental awareness features.

In terms of design, the AirPods with cameras will reportedly have longer stems than normal AirPods Pro to accommodate the cameras. There will also be a small LED light that automatically turns on when the cameras are capturing data.

The AirPods with cameras were originally slated for release in 2026. More recent reporting, however, suggests the timeline has slipped to late 2027 because of Apple Intelligence and Siri delays.

AirPods Max

Apple just updated AirPods Max earlier this year with the H2 chip, a new high-dynamic range amplifier, improved audio quality, and more.

Last year, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo reported that Apple was working on a new AirPods Max model for 2027 that is lighter than the current design. It’s unclear whether this refresh is still on the roadmap.

AirPods 5

Apple released AirPods 4 in two different variants in November 2024, including one with Active Noise Cancellation and another without. 

Most recently, Bloomberg reported that Apple is set to announce AirPods 5 at next week’s “Surprise and shine” special event, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra. 

Like AirPods 4, the new AirPods 5 are expected to come in two versions: 

with Active Noise Cancellation

without ANC

There aren’t any additional details on what new features AirPods 5 might offer. 

Wrap up: Should you buy AirPods now? 

Apple’s overall AirPods lineup is incredibly strong, especially if you can snag a pair on sale. 

That said, if you’re in the market for AirPods 4, I recommend waiting until next week to see what AirPods 5 have to offer. 

If you’re shopping for AirPods Pro 3 or AirPods Max, I think now is a great time to buy. 

AirPods Pro 3 were released last fall with a revamped in-ear fit, improved sound quality, and a built-in heart rate monitor. I think they are truly excellent. I don’t recommend waiting for AirPods with cameras right now, since those aren’t coming until sometime next year at the earliest.

title: People are sticking the Fitbit Air to their bodies, literally, and it works [Gallery]
snippet: The Fitbit Air might be one of Google’s most versatile products in a while not just because it’s so simple, but because buyers are finding very unique ways of using it. fullText:
The Fitbit Air might be one of Google’s most versatile products in a while not just because it’s so simple, but because buyers are finding very unique ways of using it. That includes quite literally sticking the Fitbit Air to your body with tape which, apparently, actually works quite well.

Google designed the Fitbit Air to be worn around your wrist, where most health trackers sit, and that’s where most buyers probably do use it. Early on, many figured out that the included band was a good way to dual-wield both the Air and a traditional watch on the same wrist, and there are dedicated products that have since come out to do that a bit more elegantly.

But another way to use the Fitbit Air? Stick it to your body, literally, with tape.

A recent thread on Reddit showed a Fitbit Air owner who started using kinesiology tape – also known as athletic tape, usually used to support sore/strained muscles – to attach the tracker to their upper arm. The subtle location is out of sight and, at least according to this user, offers “more accurate data.” That checks out, as bicep trackers can often provide slightly more accurate data by cutting out motion from the wrist, among other things. Whoop offers an official bicep band for its tracker, and there are a host of bicep bands for Fitbit Air around the web.

	

But this trend of just using some tape has been around for a little while, actually. We found a few more threads of users who have been sticking the tracker to their upper arm, and it sounds like it works out pretty well. And it’s not the only other place people are putting the tracker, as some mention putting it in their sock and elsewhere.

Google morning. How many times have you written that before? I hope you had a lovely final weekend before Labor Day. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

I think it’s safe to say that Google’s decision over the weekend to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America has been met with a bit of pushback.

	

In a blog post, Google says that it generally abides by the Geographic Names Information System when it comes to how it presents names on maps, and since Executive Order 14420 “directs the Board on Geographic Names (‘BGN’) to immediately rename Lake Ontario to Lake America and to update the Geographic Names Information System to appropriately reflect the change,” it was merely following its own protocols. Google went through the same rigmarole when it renamed Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America in February 2025.

One beneficiary of the drama has been MapQuest, the company whose rise and subsequent fall can be directly traced to Google Maps’ ascent over the past two decades. In social media posts on Friday, the company showed a cropped map of Lake Ontario with the caption, “We’re not changing it,” inspiring widespread support alongside understandable questions of “MapQuest still exists?!”

Over the weekend, the company’s Android and iOS downloads shot up 128%, bringing it to the top of their respective “maps & navigation apps” categories on both platforms, and app usage was up 50x, according to owner System1. 

As of writing, Apple has yet to make the same change to its Maps app, but it’ll likely happen any day now, particularly because the President is applying pressure, according to reports. 

Though the name change itself amounts to a minor scuffle within the larger trade war between the US and Canada, Google Maps’ enormous reach — and companies’ reliance on its APIs — means that long after the heat has died down, its effects will be felt indefinitely.

Gemini Notebook switching to compute-based usage limits, like Gemini app. Is the tool formerly known as NotebookLM so popular that Google needs to even further restrict its usage? I guess so.

Google announces ‘Expert Intelligence’ to let you add Play Books in Gemini Notebook. Gemini Notebook is becoming even more of a CliffsNotes competitor. Its new Expert Intelligence feature lets you embed participating books that you’ve purchased through Play Books into Gemini and treat them like a primary source. It’s an idea I’m curious to see authors either embrace or reject.

People are sticking the Fitbit Air to their bodies, literally, and it works [Gallery]. I kind of love this trend of seeing all the weird places people are sticking their Fitbit Airs (behave!).

🤝 Cc: David Imel

Welcome to a new project I’m calling Cc, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. First up, my friend and long-time mobile journalist, David Imel.

What do you do for fun?

For fun I do landscape photography, host community events, hike, travel, play music and spend time with my friends. My most common hobby is walking. I love walking.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

My relationship with technology is weird these days. I’ve been trying to do more things off-screen, like reading books and going to movies. I like hiking and walking because they get me off the internet. I feel that social media has been co-opted by oligarchs to make us hate each other; the more time I spend on social media, the worse I feel. Because of this, I’m trying to spend more time without any headphones in and without looking at screens, and it’s making me feel happier. I also do a lot of analog stuff like film photography and listening to records with my friends, because they feel more tangible.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

Pocket Casts. I’ve been using it for 16 years. It’s the longest app I’ve continuously used. I love it.

Viewfinder Preview and Second View. These are light meter and framing apps for my film photography. I use them all the time.

Moment Camera Pro II. I’ve been having a lot of fun taking photos on my phone and I shoot RAW through this app. It’s great.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

I’m loving the Fitbit Air. It’s nice to be able to use my analog watches but still get info about my health, especially since I’ve been taking my health more seriously this year.

What’s a recent book you loved?

I recently read both East of Eden and Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas.

East of Eden by John Steinbeck: This book is so well written. I love how wildly different the various characters are and the descriptions of Northern California.

Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas by Hunter S. Thompson: Just a wild fever dream of a book that is super fun and enjoyable to read.

What’s a recent album you loved?

The Place Behind the Stars by Streetlight Manifesto. Technically this album is only half out right now. It got delayed a few times and five of the songs are released so far. But this has been my favorite band since I discovered them in 2009 and new music from them is a blessing. The last album came out in 2013, so it’s been a long wait. The rest of the album is supposed to come out in mid-September. Currently, the album is called “Halfway to the Place Behind the Stars”.

Through This Fire Across From Peter Balkan by The Mountain Goats. This album came out last year and I love it. I was reminded of how much I loved it because The Mountain Goats just released a new album called “Days” and I did not like it much, but I listened to this one again and it is magical.

What’s a recent movie you loved?

Project Hail Mary because it was so lovely, especially in IMAX, but I also loved The Drama because of how divided it made people. And the performances were fantastic.

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

I go on very long walks every day. I usually average about 15,000 steps. I’ve also been bringing my guitar to the park almost every day and practicing it. But the #1 thing I’ve done every day since college is going to the local coffee shop every morning, catching up with the regulars and sipping some good coffee. I wake up early – usually around 7am, so it’s a really great little reprieve before the day starts.

Thank you, David, for being my guinea pig for this experiment.

The FTC and 22 US States are suing Amazon (PDF) over “secretly and systematically overcharg[ing] its approximately 1.2 million advertising customers by manipulating the ‘auctions’ that it uses to set the price of ads on its platform.” In response, Amazon says that the FTC “fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers behave” and that “there is also no harm to consumers.”

Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO was August 31st. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.” (9to5Mac)

You’ve probably heard about the proliferation of Flock cameras being deployed around the US to track everything from individuals moving around a city to car license plates. You’ve also probably heard about the similarly swift backlash from community members who are tired of being followed, harassed, and, in some cases, wrongfully arrested. A massive swath of Valve’s production Steam database from 2003 to 2013 has leaked, and with it comes a veritable treasure trove of unfinished game files, including from Portal 2, Left 4 Dead 2, and CS:GO. (Ars Technica)

The harness that started it all mere months ago, OpenClaw, is back with a massive 2.0 update. While it now has dozens of competitors, including Hermes Agent (which I prefer), it’s nice to see the OG getting a spit-shine.

fullText:
Google has quietly released a cozy mobile game called Froggy’s World in the vein of Animal Crossing and Stardew Valley.

Froggy’s World is accessed by searching “weather” on Google Search and tapping the new ‘play’ icon in the top-right corner of the Knowledge Panel card. 

There’s also a direct link here: share.google/refnf9gUiPMARpgJO. This game is only available on mobile and will not appear on desktop.

You help Google’s iconic Weather Frog spruce up their new home, which is the mushroom we’ve previously seen on the Nest Hub and other Smart Displays.

	

You pull weeds and collect tokens by tapping. The game explains how there are “different types of tokens based on the current weather”: day, night, rain, and snow. They can be exchanged for seeds and other decorative items (lamp posts, statues, etc.) that you plant to liven up your surroundings. This process will take a few days.

There are various characters that you can tap to see dialogue, while “Stash” — the recycling raccoon — is just adorable. 

The top left-corner notes your current temperature and wind conditions, as well as a token counter. The settings gear lets you switch Google Accounts (with progress saved between sessions), control the delightful background music, and sound effects. You can also reset your progress with “delete my data” at the bottom.

Game mechanics aside, Froggy’s World is hosted on dailygames.discover.google.com, which we first spotted in 2024.
